articles.title: My open source project is brand new and already has contributors. Here's what I did.
articles.description: In the spirit of Hacktoberfest, with it being the last day of October, I wanted to share my story...
articles.body_html:
In the spirit of Hacktoberfest, with it being the last day of October, I wanted to share my story about open source and building in public.

I'm a DevRel. In my day job, I help people who've never contributed to open source get their first code shipped. So when I started building answerLoops, an open source, self-hostable AI support tool, one thing bugged me. Was my own project actually easy to jump into?

What is answerLoops?

answerLoops turns your knowledge source into answers for your community. It's self-hostable, so you can run it on your own infrastructure with the AI provider you choose, or use the hosted app.

Here's the workflow:

  1. A question comes in from a community channel like Discord, Slack, Discourse, GitHub, or website chat.
  2. answerLoops searches your knowledge: your docs, files, GitHub repos, and Notion pages.
  3. It drafts a reply with the sources attached.
  4. A second AI agent checks the draft against those sources.
  5. Your team approves the reply, or you turn on auto-reply for the questions that pass the check.
  6. Useful resolutions are saved as knowledge, and knowledge gaps show what your docs are missing.

That workflow is why the labels below make sense. frontend work touches the dashboard where a team reviews and approves replies. backend work touches the pipeline and the channel integrations behind it.

Explore answerLoops on ⭐️ GitHub

The project is new, so the hard part right now is getting off the ground and getting people to find it. I posted about it on Reddit and X. It didn't bring in many stars. So I changed where I put my effort. Instead of trying to reach everyone, I focused on developers who want to build something and on making it easy for them to start.

Over the last week, developers started showing up. They sent pull requests, and I merged them. Some built something from an open issue. Others found a problem on their own and fixed it.

I can't prove any of this is cause and effect. I have a handful of data points, and some of them didn't pick up an issue at all. But I did set a few things up beforehand, and I think they're worth writing down for anyone starting out.

1. I labeled issues by skill, not just by type

At first my issues only had the usual labels: enhancement, bug, documentation. That tells a contributor what kind of change it is, but not whether it's for them.

I added two labels: frontend and backend. Right now I have 58 open issues, 41 tagged frontend and 33 tagged backend. Someone can click one label and see only the work that matches their skills, without reading all 58.

I also use good first issue and help wanted. good first issue is the one most people already know. The skill labels are the new part.

Most of the PRs I merged closed an issue with one of these labels, so they look like they're doing something. I'm still careful about how much I claim.

One side effect: only 8 good first issue tickets are open now. Labels only work while there's something behind them, so I'm writing more.

2. I wrote issues like specs

I'd have undersold this one if I'd only written about labels.

The issue my first contributor picked up was tagged frontend, good first issue, and help wanted. It was also written so that someone who had never seen the codebase could start. It had:

  • A Problem section: the data was already being collected and stored, but nothing in the UI showed it.
  • A Scope section: exactly what to show, where to start looking in the code, and what the wording should be.
  • A Not in this issue section: what to leave alone, so nobody drifts into a bigger project.
  • Acceptance criteria as a checklist.

It also said it was part of a larger tracking issue, so a contributor could see where it fit.

A vague issue like "show usage on the article page" leaves a newcomer guessing about scope, wording, and what "done" means. A scoped one lets them start. If I had to pick one thing to copy, it's this.

Every issue also ends with a link to the contributing guide, and it's now built into the Issues template.

3. I made the project easy to run

You can't contribute to something you can't start. I rewrote the README to be a short overview, and added a CONTRIBUTING guide plus issue forms for bugs, features, integrations, and docs, so new reports come in with the details I need.

The first version of the setup steps wasn't good enough. It ran the Docker path, then said "or run it natively," and I couldn't tell you which one to pick. If I was confused, a newcomer was too. I rewrote it as three steps: clone the app, set the values in one .env, and run it. Then I ran the native steps myself against a fresh database to make sure they work.

Contributors have already improved the docs from there, including a diagram of the install flow in the self-hosting quickstart.

4. Review was fast, and the PRs made it easy

The PRs came with a clear description of what changed, why, and how to try it. That made them easy to review, and I could merge quickly.

Fast feedback matters. A first-time contributor who waits two weeks for a reply rarely comes back.

5. I said thank you in public

The contributors are credited in the release notes and in the docs, and I thanked them publicly. Open source is mostly volunteers, so it's the least I can do. It also shows the next person what happens when they contribute.

I also posted on LinkedIn and X.

Thanks Aaqibhafeez Khan for the kind words

What I got wrong, or am not sure of

  • I don't know if the labels worked 100%. Nothing else about the project changed much, but I also posted about it in a few places, which brings people in on its own.
  • Not everyone took a labeled issue. Some contributors found a problem nobody had filed, and the labels can't explain that.
  • Return visits are the real test. What matters is whether people come back for a second PR.
  • The supply runs out. Contributors finish good first issue tickets quickly. Writing good ones is now a regular chore for me.

If you want to try this

  • Label issues by the skill needed, not just the type of change.
  • Write one issue as a spec: problem, scope, what's out of scope, and acceptance criteria.
  • Make sure someone can run the project, and test those steps yourself.
  • Review fast.
  • Thank people in public.

If you're new to open source and want help with a first PR, leave a comment or message me. I'm happy to walk you through it. The open issues are here: https://github.com/answerLoops/answerLoops/issues

And if you maintain a project: what got your first outside contributors to show up?

P.S. If you're reading this, starring ⭐️ the repo also really helps people find it :)

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: I Built 101 Indian Monuments in the Browser Using Only Code (No 3D Models)
articles.description: There isn't a single 3D model file on this site. Every one of these 101 monuments, from the Taj...
articles.body_html:
There isn't a single 3D model file on this site. Every one of these 101 monuments, from the Taj Mahal to a Himalayan monastery, is a small JavaScript function that builds the building out of boxes, cylinders and domes.

👉 Try it: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app ·
Code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india

The project in numbers

  • 🏛️ 101 monuments across 26 states and union territories
  • 📦 0 downloaded 3D models, 0 build steps, 0 npm dependencies for the site
  • 🪶 ~2 KB of code per monument on average (the smallest is under 1 KB)
  • 🎨 1 shader that paints stone, brick, marble and water on all of them
  • 🌙 Day and night modes, with floodlights, festival lights and stars

Why I built it

Most people can find the Taj Mahal on a map. Far fewer could place Rani ki Vav, Ramappa or Key Monastery. I wanted a way to see how widely India's architecture is spread, and to explore each building from every angle instead of scrolling through photos.

So the site opens on a map of India, not a list. Every monument is a pin, coloured by kind: 51 temples and shrines, 25 tombs and memorials, 17 forts and palaces, and 8 civic and engineering works. Click one, and the map gives way to a 3D model you can spin, zoom and step through with the arrow keys.

Every monument also has its own link, so #taj-mahal opens the Taj directly.

How a monument is born, in five steps

Step 1: Snap together simple shapes 🧱

Think of LEGO. Instead of downloading a ready-made Qutub Minar, the code stacks simple pieces: a flat box for the base, five tapering cylinders for the storeys, a ring of balconies, and a small domed pavilion on top.

Two tricks make the shapes richer than plain LEGO:

  • Lathe works like a potter's wheel. Draw half the outline of a dome, spin it, and you get the whole dome. Every onion dome on the site comes from one shared outline.
  • Extrude works like a cookie cutter pushed through dough. Draw a flat shape, such as an arch or a star-shaped platform, and the code pushes it into a thick 3D slab.

Step 2: Crimp the edges ✨

The Qutub Minar's storeys aren't smooth tubes; they have ridges (flutes). To make them, the code walks around each cylinder and pushes the wall in and out in a wave, like crimping the edge of a pie crust. Change the wave and you get a different storey: rounded flutes at the bottom, star-shaped ones higher up.

Here's the heart of it, trimmed down:

// For every point on the tier's surface...
const a = Math.atan2(z, x);                      // how far around the tower are we?
const f = 1 + 0.07 * Math.abs(Math.cos(a * 12)); // push out in 12 waves
pos.setX(k, x * f);
pos.setZ(k, z * f);

Step 3: Reuse the small pieces 🔁

Indian architecture repeats its vocabulary: chhatris (small domed pavilions), minarets, kalash finials, shikhara spires and gopuram gateways appear again and again. These all live in one shared file, js/helpers.js, so a new monument mostly combines pieces that already exist.

This is why some monuments are tiny. The whole Somnath Temple, including the sea behind it and the arrow pillar on its sea wall, is under 1 KB, because a single helper call builds the entire temple:

nagaraTemple({ w: 14, h: 26, m: STONE, shade: SHADE, plinth: 3, urus: 8,
               halls: [[18, 9, 6], [16, 8, 5]] })

Step 4: Paint it with a "magic stone" shader 🎨

Plain shapes still look like plain shapes. What makes them read as stone is the surface shader in js/surface.js, and it's the single most important idea in the project.

The problem: normally, to put a pattern on a 3D shape you "unwrap" it, like cutting gift-wrap to fit each box by hand. Doing that for every piece of 101 buildings was never going to happen.

The solution: the pattern lives in space itself. Imagine carving each building out of one giant block of marble whose veins already run through it. Wherever you cut, the pattern is there and fits perfectly. So a one-metre block is exactly the same size on the Qutub Minar as on the walls of Agra Fort, no matter how either was built.

From that one idea, the shader draws:

  • Block joints, brick courses and marble veins. Each material is tagged with a kind (masonry, marble, brick, rock, jali screen, glazed tiles, carved frieze and more).
  • Fake bumps. It shades the joints and veins with light-and-shadow hints, the way an artist shades a pencil drawing, so flat walls look grooved.
  • Weathering. Darker grime near the ground and faint rain streaks down the walls, like a film crew aging a set.
  • A tiny random tint per piece, so a row of twenty identical columns doesn't look photocopied.
  • Moving water. Four layers of gentle, drifting ripples break up the sky's reflection, the way it looks on a real pond.

For the ten best-known monuments, the shader adds grain from real photographs (free CC0 textures from Poly Haven). Picture three projectors shining a photo of real marble onto the model from the front, the side and the top. The photo's own colour is removed and only its grain is kept, then tinted to the model's colour. The Taj stays white, the Red Fort stays red, and any other monument using the same stone gets the detail for free.

Step 5: Light it like a photograph ☀️

  • A sun with soft shadows and a sky light that gently fills the shaded side.
  • A reflection of the sky for gold, bronze and polished marble to shine with.
  • Ambient occlusion darkens corners and the undersides of roofs, where light struggles to reach, like dust settling in corners.
  • Tone mapping is the camera's exposure setting, so a bright sky doesn't turn pure white.
  • Night mode switches on floodlights and festival lights, adds a soft glow (bloom) around them, and fills the sky with stars.

None of these effects is special on its own. Stacked together, they stop your eye from reading the models as boxes.

Why code instead of 3D scans?

A 3D scan is like a photo of a cake: very detailed, but megabytes per monument, with licensing questions attached. A coded model is like the recipe: a couple of kilobytes, readable by anyone, and easy to change.

Each monument also gets a "library card" in js/data.js with its name, local-script name, coordinates, dates, style, material and the recipe that builds it:

{ id: 'taj-mahal', state: 'Uttar Pradesh', lat: 27.1751, lng: 78.0421,
  type: 'memorial', name: 'Taj Mahal', local: 'ताज महल',
  built: '1632–1653', style: 'Mughal', material: 'White Makrana marble',
  build: buildTaj }

Adding the 102nd monument means writing one module and one card. That's it.

The problems I didn't expect 🐛

1. Flickering walls. When two surfaces sit in exactly the same spot (a marble band flush with a wall, the stacked slices of a temple spire), the graphics card can't decide which one is in front, so they flicker as the camera moves, like two stickers fighting over the same place. js/coplanar.js finds every clash and nudges one surface a hair forward in depth. The shapes themselves don't change.

2. Buildings on square islands. Lawns and pavements are flat boxes, so every monument looked like it was sitting on a tile with hard edges. js/landscape.js fades their open edges into the land around them, and lets seas and long rivers run on to the horizon.

3. Hills that bent temples. Rocks, hills and trees start as rough low-poly blobs. js/naturalize.js rebuilds them in more detail and roughens them with noise, like squishing clay. The first catch: a temple sitting on a hilltop got warped along with the hill. The fix was to let hills only bulge outward, so their flat tops stay flat.

4. The ocean that shimmered. A sea made of a few giant triangles loses precision far from the camera and starts to shimmer. The water is now split into tiles, at most 60 a side.

5. Phones. Ambient occlusion and water reflections are skipped on phones to keep the frame rate smooth.

Small tools, no tooling

The whole site is index.html, one stylesheet and plain ES modules, with three.js loaded from a CDN through an import map. There's no build step, no bundler and no framework, so deploying is just pushing to main on Vercel.

Looking back, this is what kept the project moving. With no dependencies to update and no build to break, every hour went into the monuments themselves.

The map isn't a tile service either. India's outline and state borders come from Natural Earth's public-domain data, simplified into SVG paths. When you pick a monument, the camera behaves like a photographer stepping back until the whole building fits in the frame, then glides there in about a second.

10 favourites, and how they were built

  1. Konark Sun Temple, Odisha. The temple is a stone chariot for the Sun god, and its 24 carved wheels work as sundials. The model rebuilds the chariot plinth on all 24 wheels from one shared wheel() helper.
  2. Hawa Mahal, Jaipur. 953 small windows let the women of the court watch the street unseen. The latticed jali holes are cut by the shader rather than modelled, so the stone stays solid and the screens still cast the right shadows.
  3. Rani ki Vav, Gujarat. A stepwell that descends seven levels. The ground is built as raised blocks so the trench can step down, landing by landing, to the well.
  4. Lotus Temple, Delhi. Its 27 marble petals are built from a single curved petal() shape, repeated in three rings and rotated into place.
  5. Meenakshi Temple, Madurai. Its gateway towers are covered in painted figures. Each gopuram uses a random seed, so every tower gets its own pattern of colours.
  6. Qutub Minar, Delhi. Five storeys, four different kinds of flutes, all from the "pie-crust" trick above.
  7. Statue of Unity, Gujarat. The world's tallest statue, built from smooth, rounded forms: the dhoti's folds, the shawl over the shoulders and half-closed hands.
  8. Taj Mahal, Agra. Onion domes from the shared lathe outline, plus the charbagh garden and its reflecting pool.
  9. Somnath Temple, Gujarat. The whole model is under 1 KB, thanks to the shared temple helper.
  10. Ramappa Temple, Telangana. One of the few Indian temples named after its sculptor, with a tower built of bricks light enough to float.

See all 101 on the live map. There's also an 8½-minute film of every monument, five seconds each, rendered from the site's own models; the project is in the repo's video/ folder.

Try it, break it, add to it

  • 🗺️ Explore: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app. Try finding Key Monastery on the map without searching.
  • ⭐ Read the code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india. Run it locally with npx serve .
  • 💬 Tell me in the comments: which monument should be #102?

These models are interpretations, not survey records. Anyone who has stood in front of the Kailasa Temple will see what they simplify. The goal is a sense of form, scale and place, and for that, code plus a good shader goes a long way.

Credits: three.js (MIT licence). Photo textures: CC0 from Poly Haven. Map data: Natural Earth, public domain. This article was drafted with AI assistance from the project's source.

articles.title: Neon Realtime vs Supabase Realtime
articles.description: Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up...
articles.body_html:
Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up to date as the data changes. Neon hasn't published latency numbers yet, so I measured it.

I compared it with polling, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and both flavors of Supabase Realtime, on 10,000 and 1,000,000 rows. Everything ran on October 28, 2026 in Frankfurt.

TL;DR

Median time from UPDATE to an up-to-date result on the client, at 10k and 1M rows:

  • Neon Realtime: 40–46 ms for filters, joins and top-10 queries. That's one network round trip from my laptop. The change usually arrived within 8 ms of the write's commit ack.
  • Supabase Broadcast: 58–60 ms on a plain filter. Joins and top-10 need a refetch, so 108–115 ms.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: 70–244 ms. Every change costs a second query.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: 328–434 ms, and 1.1 s for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Polling every second: 414–546 ms, change or not.
  • The large aggregate used more bandwidth. At 1M rows, Neon still had the lowest latency at 179 ms, but re-sent the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB per change.
  • Scale-to-zero still works. The compute suspended with a subscription open and stayed suspended for the 10 minutes I watched. The subscription stayed live and got the next write.

What Neon Realtime does

Your server defines the query and seals it into a token that expires after 60 seconds. The browser subscribes with that token over a WebSocket. Neon sends the full result once, then only the changes.

// Server: the query and its parameters stay on your side
import { createRealtime, rawSql } from "@neon/realtime/server";

const realtime = createRealtime({ secret: process.env.NEON_REALTIME_SECRET, db: "neondb" });
const sealed = await realtime.seal({
  query: rawSql("SELECT id, name, score FROM players WHERE team_id = $1", [teamId]),
});
// send `sealed` to the browser

// Browser
import { createRealtimeClient } from "@neon/realtime/client";

const client = createRealtimeClient({ url: NEON_REALTIME_URL });
const subscription = client.subscribe(sealed);
subscription.onChange(({ data }) => render(data));

The client asks your server for a fresh token before the old one expires. The React bindings and QueryRefreshController do that for you.

Limits in the beta:

  • Queries: read-only and deterministic, so no now() or gen_random_uuid(). Joins, aggregates, ORDER BY … LIMIT, subqueries and window functions are supported.
  • Tables: every table needs a primary key.
  • Auth: no row-level security yet. You authorize when you seal the query.
  • Regions: four AWS regions (us-east-1, us-east-2, eu-central-1, ap-southeast-1).
  • Price: Realtime is free during the beta. Compute and egress are billed as usual.

The setup

  • Neon: 0.25 CU (1 GB RAM), Postgres 18.6, aws-eu-central-1.
  • Supabase: Nano instance (0.5 GB RAM, shared CPU), Postgres 17.11, eu-central-1.
  • Client: my laptop, about 40 ms round trip from Frankfurt. That round trip is the floor for every number below.

Both are the smallest compute on their platform. The Supabase project was on the Free plan. The Neon project sat in my Launch-plan org, but Neon's Free plan runs the same 0.25 CU with the same 5-minute scale-to-zero, and the whole benchmark used 0.43 CU-hours of the 100 a month it includes.

The Postgres versions were the defaults. Neon created the project on Postgres 18. Hosted Supabase tops out at 17.11 as of this writing.

The table is players(id, name, team_id, score) with 1,000 teams. Each write is UPDATE players SET score = $1 WHERE id = 1 over an open direct connection. Then I timed how long the subscriber took to see the new score.

Five ways to keep a query live:

  1. Neon Realtime: subscribe to the SQL query.
  2. Supabase Broadcast: a trigger calls realtime.broadcast_changes() into a private channel. Supabase recommends it "for scalability and security".
  3. LISTEN/NOTIFY on Neon: a trigger sends NOTIFY, and the app re-runs the query.
  4. Supabase Postgres Changes: subscribe to row changes on players.
  5. Polling on Neon: re-run the query every second.

The four queries:

  • Filter: the players in one team. 10 rows at 10k, 1,000 rows at 1M.
  • Join: the same players joined with teams.
  • Aggregate: player count and top score for every team (1,000 groups).
  • Top 10: the 10 highest scores across all players.

With both Supabase methods, the client applies the changed row itself for the filter. A change event alone can't update a join, an aggregate or a top 10, so for those the client refetches the query over the REST API.

How I measured
  • One Node process runs the writer and the subscriber, so both timestamps come from the same clock.
  • Write to screen is the time from sending the UPDATE until the subscriber's copy of the result contains the new score. It includes any refetch the method needs.
  • 5 warm-up writes, then 100 writes per cell with a random 250–750 ms gap. Timeout 10 s. Nothing timed out.
  • The Supabase refetches query views through supabase-js, with RLS on and a public read policy.
  • Bytes per change are the WebSocket bytes received plus the size of any refetched result.
  • One writer, one subscriber. I didn't test fan-out to many subscribers.

Write to screen

The differences come down to how many trips a change takes to reach the screen:

  • Neon Realtime: the change arrived between 2 ms before and 8 ms after the writer got its commit ack. So it's as fast as the network allows. The exception is the aggregate at 1M rows (next section).
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: the notification arrives about as fast as Realtime, then the query runs a second time. At 1M rows the filter returns 1,000 rows (64 KB), so it climbs to 159 ms.
  • Supabase Broadcast: the event arrived ~57 ms after the write in every cell. The REST refetch added 50–70 ms, and ~740 ms for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: the event alone took 315–384 ms. Supabase's docs say it processes changes on a single thread and checks RLS for every subscriber, and that it "does not scale as well" as Broadcast.
  • Polling: on average you wait half the interval, plus the query. It also runs 86,400 queries a day per client, even when nothing changes.

Getting the first result after subscribing took 0.4–0.8 s on Neon Realtime and 0.8–1.4 s on Supabase Broadcast, including the WebSocket handshake.

At 1–2 writes a second, the write itself took ~40 ms with every method. A live query didn't slow down the writer.

p50 / p95 tables (ms)
10,000 rows
Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 40 / 56 40 / 48 44 / 51 42 / 123
Supabase Broadcast 58 / 62 110 / 122 125 / 196 108 / 125
LISTEN/NOTIFY 84 / 90 83 / 87 128 / 207 85 / 315
Supabase Postgres Changes 371 / 569 397 / 619 418 / 642 368 / 615
Polling every 1 s 484 / 724 534 / 731 546 / 700 498 / 708

1,000,000 rows

Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 44 / 52 41 / 54 179 / 191 46 / 74
Supabase Broadcast 60 / 249 115 / 132 793 / 856 110 / 121
LISTEN/NOTIFY 159 / 176 145 / 155 244 / 269 70 / 74
Supabase Postgres Changes 328 / 540 418 / 626 1129 / 1293 434 / 633
Polling every 1 s 542 / 723 495 / 740 517 / 732 414 / 709

Bytes per change

For filters and joins, Neon sends only the changed row, ~0.4 KB per change, whatever the table size. A refetch downloads the whole result again: 64–73 KB per change at 1M rows.

The large aggregate exposes Neon's bandwidth tradeoff. At 10k rows, each change arrived as a ~0.4 KB delta. At 1M rows the engine switched to re-sending the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB and 179 ms per change. That's more than twice the data transferred by a refetch. Neon's docs warn that "complex queries add write-processing latency, especially on larger datasets."

Top 10 re-sends the full result on every change too, but that's only 1.8 KB.

Supabase's aggregate refetch took ~740 ms after the event at 1M rows. Part of that is the Nano instance: the same query took ~200 ms on Neon's 0.25 CU. Bigger Supabase compute would help.

Scale to zero

Neon suspends a compute after 5 minutes without queries. I opened a Realtime subscription while the compute was suspended, then left it alone (twice). For comparison, I did the same with a plain LISTEN connection.

  • The subscription woke the compute: first result in 1.3–2.5 s.
  • The compute suspended anyway, 5.3–5.4 minutes later, with the subscription open.
  • It stayed suspended. In the second run I watched for 10 more minutes. The compute never woke, though the subscription's token renewed every minute.
  • The subscription stayed live. A write to the sleeping database woke it (ack in 917–965 ms, most of it connecting), and the subscriber had the change 9–48 ms after the ack.
  • LISTEN didn't block suspension either, but Neon terminated the connection after 5 min 18 s (57P01). The registration is gone, notifications sent before you reconnect are lost, and reconnecting wakes the compute again.

So an open dashboard tab doesn't keep the database billing. Polling does, because it never stops querying.

Caveats

  • One subscriber and one writer at 1–2 writes a second. Fan-out and heavy write load are untested.
  • Every number includes a ~40 ms round trip from my laptop. A server in the same region would see lower numbers everywhere.
  • Supabase's Nano has half the RAM of Neon's 0.25 CU and a shared CPU. That affects refetch-heavy cells, not event delivery.
  • Neon Realtime is a beta. Neon says the protocol isn't stable yet.
  • One run per configuration, on one day.

Which one should you use?

  • Neon Realtime: live results of real queries (lists, joins, leaderboards, per-user views) on Neon. Watch large aggregates, and authorize at seal time until RLS lands.
  • Supabase Broadcast: you're on Supabase and the client can apply the changed row itself.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: any Postgres, a small result, and you're fine with a refetch per change. On Neon, reconnect after the compute suspends.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: prototypes. Supabase itself points you to Broadcast.
  • Polling: when a few seconds of delay is fine and the database is awake anyway.

Sources

Checked October 28, 2026.

  • Neon: Realtime launch, overview, how it works, queries, subscribing, compute lifecycle, LISTEN/NOTIFY guide
  • Supabase: subscribing to database changes, Postgres Changes, changelog
  • Charts: rendered from the raw results with Pele

articles.title: Debugging in the Agentic Era
articles.description: Coding agents write frontend code fast, but they can't see it run. This is the flow I use to fix...
articles.body_html:
Coding agents write frontend code fast, but they can't see it run. This is the flow I use to fix that, with a signup form that fails on submit as the example.

The Old Way

  1. The agent changes the form.
  2. You open the page, click submit, and nothing happens.
  3. You open DevTools, find a 422 in the Network tab, and copy the response.
  4. You paste it into the chat. The agent guesses a fix.
  5. You reload. Now the console shows a TypeError. You copy and paste again.

You're the agent's eyes, and most of your time goes to copying, not thinking.

The New Way

  1. You ask: "Submit the signup form on localhost:3000 and tell me why it fails."
  2. The agent clicks submit, reads the 422 response and the console, and matches them to the code.
  3. It explains the cause and proposes a fix.
  4. You check that explanation against what you see in the browser, then approve or push back. 
flowchart TB
  accTitle: The old way and the new way
  accDescr: In the old way, the agent writes code, the browser shows an error, and you copy that error back to the agent. In the new way, the agent reads the browser through MCP and reports its findings to you, and you validate them before it continues.
  subgraph Old
    direction TB
    a1[Agent] -- writes code --> b1[Browser]
    b1 -- error --> y1[You]
    y1 -- paste --> a1
  end
  subgraph New
    direction TB
    a2[Agent] -- writes code --> b2[Browser]
    b2 -- MCP --> a2
    a2 -- findings --> y2[You]
    y2 -- validate --> a2
  end
  Old ~~~ New

The copy-paste is gone. You're still there, in a different role.

This is human in the loop (HITL): the agent gathers evidence, and you validate it. Don't trust it 100%. It can misread a trace, or silence an error instead of fixing it.

The HITL notes in this post mark where to look yourself.

Cover Every Scenario

Browser access lets the agent put a page through every scenario your customers hit, not only the one where everything works:

Scenario What the customer should get
Success The flow works end to end
Slow A loading state, no double submits
Error A clear message, their input kept, a retry
Performance Fast loading, no layout shifts
Accessibility Works with a keyboard and a screen reader

The rest of this post shows how to set it up, then walks through each one.

The Tools

Two MCP servers give an agent a browser. MCP is an open standard, so neither is tied to Claude Code. Both work in Cursor, VS Code with Copilot, Codex, and Gemini CLI.

Chrome DevTools MCP

Chrome DevTools MCP is Google's MCP server for Chrome. It lets the agent open pages, click, and read what you see in DevTools:

  • Console: errors, warnings, and logs
  • Network: requests, status codes, and payloads
  • Performance: traces with Core Web Vitals like LCP and CLS
  • Accessibility: Lighthouse audits and the accessibility tree
  • Emulation: slow networks, offline mode, CPU throttling, dark mode, reduced motion, and forced colors

Playwright MCP

Playwright MCP is Microsoft's MCP server for browser automation. It drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, can make a single request fail, and helps the agent write end-to-end tests you can rerun.

Installing Them

Most agents read the same config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    },
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--caps=network"]
    }
  }
}

The --caps=network flag turns on Playwright MCP's request mocking. In Cursor, add the config under Settings > MCP. In VS Code, both READMEs have one-click install buttons.

In Claude Code, two commands add both:

claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest
claude mcp add playwright -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --caps=network

Run /mcp to confirm they're connected. Then ask the agent to open your local app and list the console messages.

By default, Chrome DevTools MCP starts its own Chrome. To use the one you already have open, add --autoConnect. It needs Chrome 144 or later, with remote debugging allowed at chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging.

Which One When

Use both, for different jobs. Chrome DevTools MCP looks inside one page: debugging, comparing, and measuring. Playwright MCP fails requests on purpose and writes tests you can rerun in any browser.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a browser MCP server
  accDescr: To debug, compare pages, or measure performance in Chrome, use Chrome DevTools MCP. To write end-to-end tests, mock failed requests, or check Firefox and Safari, use Playwright MCP.
  need{What do you need?}
  need -- "debug, compare,<br>measure" --> devtools[Chrome DevTools MCP]
  need -- "e2e tests, mocks,<br>other browsers" --> playwright[Playwright MCP]

The Debug Loop

Start with the success path: the flow working end to end. With browser access, getting there follows the same loop every time.

The agent changes the code, reloads the page, and reads the signals. You review what it found and steer it when it chases the wrong cause.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: The debug loop
  accDescr: The agent edits the code, reloads the page, and reads the console, network, and performance trace. You review what it found. If the issue isn't fixed, you steer the agent and it edits again. When it's fixed, you ship.
  edit[Agent edits code] --> reload[Reload page] --> read[Agent reads signals]
  read --> review[You review findings]
  review --> fixed{Fixed?}
  fixed -- no, you steer --> edit
  fixed -- yes --> ship[Ship]

HITL: Keep the browser window visible while the agent works. When it says the bug is fixed, reproduce it yourself before you believe it.

The two signals you'll read most are console errors and network requests.

Console Errors

My prompt: "Open /signup, submit the form, and list the console errors. Explain the cause before changing anything."

The agent reads the error and its stack trace, opens the file it points to, and tells you what it thinks went wrong. You read that explanation before any code changes.

HITL: An error that disappears isn't always fixed. Check the diff: the agent may have wrapped it in a try/catch or removed the code that logged it.

Network Requests

My prompt: "Submit the form and show me the request and response for /api/signup. Compare the payload with what the backend expects."

The agent lists the requests, opens the failing one, and compares its body with the code that builds it. A misnamed field or a missing header shows up right there.

HITL: Check the request against the API spec, not the agent's reading of it. Changing the frontend to accept a broken response hides a backend bug.

Testing Slow and Failing Requests

Customers rarely see a crash. They see a failure handled badly: a spinner that never stops, a blank page, a form that loses what they typed. The agent can slow things down or break them on purpose and show you what customers see.

Each server does this differently:

  • Playwright MCP fails one request: browser_route makes an endpoint return a 500, a 404, or a malformed body.
  • Chrome DevTools MCP degrades the whole page: emulate sets Slow 3G, offline mode, or CPU throttling. It can't mock a single request.

My prompt, combining both: "Make POST /api/signup return a 500, submit the form, and screenshot what the user sees. Then try it on Slow 3G."

Slow

On Slow 3G or with the CPU throttled, check what the customer gets:

  • A loading state that shows up right away and ends, with an error if it takes too long
  • A submit button they can't press twice
  • Content that doesn't jump around when it arrives

Error

With a request failing, check what the customer gets:

  • A message in plain words that says what to do next, not a stack trace or raw JSON
  • Their input still in the form
  • A retry that works
  • Focus moved to the error, and the error announced to screen readers

Once a state looks right, lock it in with Playwright's page.route() so it stays that way:

test('signup keeps the input and offers a retry when the API fails', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.route('**/api/signup', (route) => route.fulfill({ status: 500 }));
  await page.goto('/signup');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('ada@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Try again');
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Email')).toHaveValue('ada@example.com');
});

HITL: The agent can confirm an error message appears. Only you can judge whether it helps. Read each error state as a customer would: is it clear, kind, and does it say what to do next?

Improving Core Web Vitals

Slow requests are one side of speed. The other is how fast the page loads and settles, and that's where browser access helps most.

Without it, the agent guesses from the code. With it, the agent records a trace, sees which element is the LCP and what shifts the layout, and measures again after each change.

My prompt: "Record a performance trace of the home page with the CPU throttled 4x. Tell me the LCP element and what shifts the layout, then suggest one change at a time."

That turns "this might be faster" into numbers. The agent proposes a change, reruns the trace, and keeps it only if LCP or CLS improves.

HITL: Read the trace yourself before accepting a change. One run is noise, so ask for several. And the trade-offs are yours: preloading an image or inlining CSS can win a metric and cost something else.

Checking Accessibility

An accessible page works for every customer: people on a keyboard, on a screen reader, or who need more contrast or less motion. The agent can check part of this in the browser.

Chrome DevTools MCP runs a Lighthouse audit and reads the accessibility tree, the names and roles a screen reader announces. It also turns on the settings some customers rely on: forced colors, higher contrast, and reduced motion.

My prompt: "Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit on /signup, then tab through the form and tell me where the focus goes."

Lock the fixes in with axe in your Playwright tests:

import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('signup has no detectable accessibility violations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});

HITL: Automated checks catch only some accessibility issues. A clean audit doesn't mean the page works with a screen reader. Tab through it yourself, and try VoiceOver or NVDA on the flows that matter.

Migrating Legacy Code Without Regressions

A migration has to keep every scenario working. The worst migration bug is a new page that looks almost like the old one, so capture how the legacy page behaves before you change anything.

Start with a Contract

Write down what must stay the same. This is the contract, and every test after it checks against it.

## Contract: /checkout

- Same visible text and layout at 390px and 1280px
- Same API requests, in the same order, with the same payloads
- No new console errors or warnings
- LCP and CLS no worse than the legacy page
- Every action reachable with the keyboard

The idea is the same as in MigFlow: agents need a contract, not a tutorial.

HITL: You write or approve the contract. The agent can draft it from the legacy page, but it can't know which behavior your users depend on.

Cover the Legacy Page with Tests

Many legacy projects have no end-to-end tests. With Playwright MCP, the agent walks through the legacy page in a real browser and writes a Playwright test for each line of the contract.

Run them against the legacy page first. They must pass there, so they describe what the page does today, quirks included.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() saves screenshots of the legacy page as the baseline. Visual changes then show up as a pixel diff, not a judgment call:

test('checkout looks the same as the legacy page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', { fullPage: true });
});

Create the baseline from the legacy page with npx playwright test --update-snapshots. After that, every run compares against it.

HITL: Read every test. A test that passes no matter what protects nothing. Some quirks it captures are bugs you'll want to fix, not keep.

Migrate and Rerun the Same Tests

Now migrate, and run the same tests against the new page. A failing test is a regression. When one fails, the agent uses Chrome DevTools MCP to compare both pages and find out why.

The tests stay in CI after the migration, so the next change is covered too.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Migrating without regressions
  accDescr: Write the contract, then cover the legacy page with Playwright tests. Migrate the code and run the same tests. If they fail, debug with Chrome DevTools MCP and migrate again. When they pass, you review and ship.
  contract[Write the contract] --> cover[Test the legacy page]
  cover --> migrate[Migrate the code]
  migrate --> pass{Same tests pass?}
  pass -- no --> debug[Debug with DevTools MCP]
  debug --> migrate
  pass -- yes --> review[You review and ship]

HITL: When a test fails, you decide whether the page or the test is wrong. Don't let the agent update a screenshot baseline or loosen an assertion to go green without your OK.

Limits

  • The agent can be confidently wrong. It will explain a wrong cause as clearly as a right one.
  • It's slower than reading the code when the bug is obvious.
  • Traces and logs fill the context window, so ask for the specific signal you need.
  • The agent can read cookies and local storage. Add --isolated for a temporary profile, and be careful with --autoConnect, which uses the Chrome you're signed in to.
  • Performance traces may send page URLs to Google's CrUX API. Add --no-performance-crux when you debug internal URLs.

Try It

Start with one prompt in any agent: "Open localhost:3000, list the console errors, and explain the cause before fixing anything."

Then try the other scenarios on one page: "Load the checkout page on Slow 3G, then with the payment request failing, and screenshot what the customer sees in each case."

Migrating a page? Write the contract, then ask: "Write Playwright tests for this contract and run them against the legacy page." Run the same tests after the migration.

A Tool in the Engineer's Hands

Success, slow, error, performance, accessibility: the agent can now put a page through every scenario and bring you the evidence. That's a powerful tool in the engineer's hands.

It doesn't decide what the evidence means. Every HITL note above comes down to the same habit: keep your eyes on the browser, and treat the agent's conclusions as claims to check, not facts.

As I wrote in AI Writes Code. You Own Quality., speed without judgment means shipping bugs faster. Browser access doesn't change who owns the fix. It gives you better evidence to own it with.

The agent gets eyes on the browser. You keep the judgment.

articles.title: We took over ChatGPT accounts: the MathLive postMessage chain, and the 20-line audit for your own listeners
articles.description: A shared ChatGPT link, a math keyboard library listening to any sender, an iframe that inherits chatgpt.com, a CSP bypass through YouTube's oembed, and the session token: full account takeover, fixed Oct 26, $5k bounty. The attack chain step by step, and a static audit I ran against the vulnerable library itself: 4 listeners, zero sender checks.
articles.body_html:
Yesterday's disclosure from Parameter is the most elegant web exploit of the month: a complete takeover of ChatGPT accounts where the victim's only action was opening a shared-conversation link. No paste, no login, no click in the final version: about 4.5 seconds from link to JavaScript running as chatgpt.com, reading private conversations and the session token. Reported October 18, escalated from P2 to P1 on October 21, fixed October 26, bounty $5,000. The root is a class of bug almost every web app ships today, which is why this post is the chain dissected step by step, plus a 100-line static audit I wrote and ran against the vulnerable library: it flags exactly the four listeners that made this possible, and your codebase can be scanned the same way tonight.

The chain, in seven moves

The ingredient list: a shared conversation (public feature), MathLive (the math input library ChatGPT loads when a message contains an interactive graph), and the HTML Preview pane that runs on a separate sandboxed origin.

  1. The lure. Attacker shares a conversation containing a real interactive graph (which makes chatgpt.com load MathLive and install its virtual-keyboard message listener) plus an HTML block.
  2. The unguarded door. The sandboxed HTML Preview sends postMessage calls. MathLive's listener never checked who the message came from ("from any web address", per the researchers) and accepted a update-setting message carrying attacker-controlled HTML in the keyboard layouts[].markup field, then a show message.
  3. The sink. The layout renders through keyboardContainer.innerHTML, via a createHTML helper that was a Trusted Types wrapper or identity function, not a sanitizer. I verified the sink in the shipped bundle: s.innerHTML = Qi.createHTML(a) and friends, still present in MathLive 0.100.0.
  4. The origin inheritance. The injected payload is an <iframe srcdoc> without a sandbox attribute. A srcdoc iframe inherits the embedding document's origin: the new frame is chatgpt.com.
  5. The CSP bypass. The Content-Security-Policy blocked inline scripts but allowed YouTube. So the payload loads www.youtube.com/oembed?...&callback=<js>;void, a JSONP-style response whose body begins with attacker-chosen JavaScript. CSP sees a fetch to youtube.com, allowed. The browser executes the callback as script.
  6. The token. Running as chatgpt.com, the code reads the session bootstrap data from the page (#client-bootstrap) and obtains the access token.
  7. The takeover. With the token: GET /backend-api/conversations..., enumerate, read, exfiltrate via an innocent-looking image request. "Any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account."

Every individual piece is a textbook finding. The lesson is the composition: a library's lax listener plus a sandboxed pane plus a permissive CSP plus an unsandboxed srcdoc equals account takeover on the most-visited AI site on earth.

The audit: your listeners, tonight

The bug class has a signature: addEventListener('message', ...) handlers that never reference event.origin or event.source. I wrote a static scanner around that signature (heuristic, minified-bundle-friendly, ~100 lines) and ran it on the two things that matter:

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py mathlive-0.100.0.mjs
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2841 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2931 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:2931 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)
[RISK] mathlive-0.100.0.mjs:3084 message listener -> NO SENDER CHECK (.origin/.source absent)

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py mathlive-0.111.1.mjs        # current release
(no message listeners flagged in the main bundle)

$ python3 postmessage_audit.py ~/code/my-app/src/           # your turn

The core of the check (full script embedded below, self-contained):

PATTERNS = [re.compile(r"addEventListener\(\s*['\"`]message['\"`]\s*,"),
            re.compile(r"onmessage\s*=")]
ORIGIN_OK = re.compile(r"(?:event|e|ev|msg|evt)\.(?:origin|source)\b")
DANGEROUS = re.compile(r"innerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|outerHTML|\beval\(|new Function\(")
# for each listener: extract the handler body; flag if ORIGIN_OK absent,
# and flag louder if a DOM sink lives inside the same handler

Honest limits: it is a heuristic on source text (proxy handlers, wrapped frameworks or dynamically-registered listeners can slip through), a clean scan is not a proof, and the runtime gold standard is opening DevTools and watching which listeners react to a synthetic postMessage from a foreign origin. But the pattern it flags is precisely the one that cost OpenAI a P1 this month, and it catches the version that had it while passing the one that does not.

The full script (drop it in a repo or run it in CI over your frontend bundles):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# postmessage_audit.py <file-or-dir> [...] : flag message listeners without sender checks
import re, sys
from pathlib import Path
RX = [re.compile(r"addEventListener\(\s*['\"`]message['\"`]\s*,"), re.compile(r"onmessage\s*=")]
ORIGIN = re.compile(r"(?:event|e|ev|msg|message|evt)\.(?:origin|source)\b")
SINK = re.compile(r"innerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|outerHTML|\beval\(|new Function\(")
def scan(path):
    try: text = path.read_text(errors="replace")
    except Exception: return
    for rx in RX:
        for m in rx.finditer(text):
            win = text[m.end():m.end()+2000]; depth=0; body=""
            for i,ch in enumerate(win):
                if ch=="{": depth+=1
                elif ch=="}":
                    depth-=1
                    if depth==0: body=win[:i+1]; break
            else: body=win[:1500]
            line = text[:m.start()].count("\n")+1
            v=[]
            if not ORIGIN.search(body): v.append("NO SENDER CHECK")
            if SINK.search(body): v.append("DOM sink in handler")
            if v: print(f"[RISK] {path.name}:{line} -> {'; '.join(v)}")
for a in sys.argv[1:]:
    p=Path(a)
    for f in (sorted(p.rglob("*")) if p.is_dir() else [p]):
        if f.suffix in {".js",".mjs",".ts",".jsx",".tsx",".html",".vue",".svelte"}: scan(f)

The four defenses, in order of leverage

  1. Check the sender, always. First line of every message handler: if (event.origin !== EXPECTED) return;. One line, kills the entire class. That line was missing in a library embedded in one of the world's top websites.
  2. A Trusted Types wrapper that sanitizes, or nothing. createHTML that passes bytes through is a compliance badge on an open door. If you adopt Trusted Types, the policy must actually constrain (DOMPurify or equivalent), not just wrap.
  3. Sandbox your srcdocs. An <iframe srcdoc> without sandbox inherits your origin. sandbox="allow-scripts" (no allow-same-origin) makes the injected document powerless against yours. The preview pane was sandboxed; the attacker's frame was not.
  4. CSP is a budget, audit the allowed list. Any endpoint echoing a callback parameter is a script-execution primitive (JSONP is not dead, it lives in oembed endpoints). youtube.com in a CSP is not "just videos": read it as "YouTube decides what JavaScript runs on my page".

What this means for AI platforms specifically

The trust model of an AI chat app is unusual: user-generated content becomes application UI (shared conversations render graphs, previews, embeds inside the first-party origin). Every library the platform loads to render that content inherits the platform's authority, and the attacker gets to choose which content triggers which library. OpenAI's fix (rejecting cross-frame MathLive messages plus CSP changes) is correct and shipped in eight days. The $5,000 bounty for a full account takeover on the flagship product is, let us note in passing, a curious pricing signal.

TL;DR: a shared ChatGPT link + MathLive's message listener that trusted any sender + innerHTML sink + unsandboxed srcdoc + YouTube JSONP CSP bypass = the session token and every private conversation, patched October 26. The bug class is addEventListener('message') without an origin check; the 100-line audit above flags it in your bundles (and correctly flagged the vulnerable MathLive while passing the fixed one). One line of event.origin validation per listener is the whole vaccine.

Sources: Parameter: We took over ChatGPT accounts · MathLive · audit verified against mathlive 0.100.0 (4 listeners, no sender checks, innerHTML sinks present) and 0.111.1 (pattern absent from main bundle)

articles.title: Next.js 16 `use cache` Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces
articles.description: Next.js 16 replaces implicit caching with explicit use cache directives. Learn function-level caching, cacheLife profiles, migration from unstable_cache, and production cache storage patterns.
articles.body_html:
Next.js 16 use cache Directive: Granular Caching at the Function Level and What It Replaces

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Next.js 16 eliminates the framework's most confusing aspect: implicit caching. Previous versions cached fetch requests automatically, left developers guessing when route segments became static, and buried cache configuration inside fetch options. The new use cache directive makes every cache decision explicit. Developers mark what to cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag().

The old model failed because developers could not predict cache behavior. A fetch call with no options might cache forever or not cache at all, depending on whether the route contained dynamic functions. Route segments became static or dynamic based on heuristics the compiler inferred from your code. Production bugs emerged when a component that worked dynamically in development suddenly rendered statically in production, serving stale data for hours.

Problem: implicit caching causes unpredictable cache behavior and stale data

Next.js 16 solves this with use cache. When you add the directive to a function or component, the framework caches its return value. When you call cacheLife('hours'), the cache expires in one hour. When you call cacheTag(['products']), you can invalidate that cache entry on demand. The mental model becomes: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation.

Solution: explicit use cache directive gives predictable control

This post covers what use cache replaces, how function-level and component-level caching work, migration patterns from unstable_cache, the cache hierarchy Next.js now uses, and production gotchas around cache storage.

Key Takeaways

  • use cache replaces unstable_cache, fetch cache options, and all implicit caching; every cache decision is now explicit.
  • You can cache at the function level (data fetching) or component level (entire UI trees), with arguments and closures becoming part of the cache key automatically.
  • cacheLife() sets expiration windows; cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation; both pair with use cache to control freshness.
  • Cache storage defaults to in-memory per instance; use cache: remote moves entries to a shared durable handler for high hit rates.
  • Migration requires converting unstable_cache wrappers to use cache directives and replacing fetch next.revalidate with cacheLife() calls.

What use cache Replaces: unstable_cache, fetch Options, and Implicit Caching

use cache supersedes three caching mechanisms from Next.js 15 and earlier.

unstable_cache: developers wrapped functions in unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, options) to cache database queries or API calls. The wrapper returned a new function that memoized results. The name signaled instability; the API never graduated to stable. Next.js 16 removes it entirely.

fetch cache options: developers passed { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } to fetch calls to cache HTTP responses. The framework intercepted fetch, stored the response in a data cache, and served cached data until expiration. This worked only for fetch calls. Database queries and third-party SDK calls required unstable_cache.

Implicit route caching: Next.js analyzed route segments at build time. If a segment contained no dynamic functions (cookies, headers, searchParams), the compiler marked it static and prerendered it. If any child component called a dynamic function, the entire segment became dynamic. Developers could not see this decision; they inferred it from build output or production behavior.

All three mechanisms are gone. use cache handles every scenario.

Diagram showing old caching mechanisms replaced by use cache

The removal creates a single model. You mark cacheable operations with use cache, set expiration with cacheLife(), and invalidate with cacheTag(). The compiler generates cache keys from function arguments and captured closures. No wrapper functions, no fetch-specific options, no implicit heuristics.

This unification matters because developers now reason about caching the same way everywhere. A database query, a fetch call, and a React Server Component all use identical syntax. The cache key derivation follows the same rules. The expiration model applies uniformly.

How use cache Works: Function-Level and Component-Level Caching

The use cache directive applies to async functions and React Server Components. When Next.js encounters it, the framework serializes the function's return value into an RSC payload and stores that payload in a cache.

Function-level caching targets data operations. Add use cache to the top of an async function that fetches from a database, calls a third-party API, or performs expensive computation:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const product = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1',
    [id]
  );

  return product;
}

The compiler generates a cache key from the function identity and its arguments. In this example, the key includes getProduct and the id value. Calling getProduct('123') creates one cache entry; calling getProduct('456') creates another. The framework does not cache the function itself; it caches the result for each unique set of arguments.

Component-level caching targets UI trees. Add use cache to an async component that renders JSX:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductList() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const products = await db.query('SELECT * FROM products');

  return (
    <ul>
      {products.map(product => (
        <li key={product.id}>{product.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

The framework caches the entire RSC payload for the component. The payload includes the rendered JSX, serialized props, and any data the component loaded. When Next.js renders the same component again within the cache window, it returns the cached payload without executing the component body.

Content image showing cache key generation and payload storage

How use cache generates keys and stores payloads

The cache key includes arguments and any values captured from parent scopes. If a component reads a variable from a closure, that variable becomes part of the key. This ensures different inputs produce separate cache entries.

Arguments and return values must be serializable. You cannot cache functions, class instances with methods, or objects containing Symbols. The framework serializes primitives, plain objects, arrays, and React elements. Attempting to cache non-serializable values throws a runtime error.

Components marked with use cache cannot directly call cookies(), headers(), or access searchParams. These APIs provide request-time data that varies per request. Calling them inside a cached function creates a contradiction: the cache expects stable inputs, but runtime APIs return dynamic values. If you need runtime data, pass it as an argument to the cached function from a non-cached parent component.

Using cacheLife() for Granular Cache Control

cacheLife() sets the expiration policy for a cached function. Without it, Next.js applies a default profile. The default provides basic time-based invalidation, but production apps need explicit control.

The function accepts a named profile or a custom configuration object. Next.js 16 ships with four built-in profiles:

Profile Revalidate Expire Stale
seconds 15 seconds 15 seconds 1 minute
minutes 5 minutes 5 minutes 1 hour
hours 1 hour 1 hour 1 day
days 1 day 1 day 7 days

Revalidate determines when the cache entry becomes stale. After this window, Next.js marks the entry for refresh but continues serving the stale value while fetching a new one in the background.

Expire sets the hard limit. After this window, the cache entry becomes invalid. Requests cannot use it; Next.js must fetch fresh data synchronously.

Stale controls client-side caching. The browser keeps the RSC payload fresh for this duration when prefetching or navigating.

Use a built-in profile when the default windows fit your data freshness requirements:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

Use a custom configuration when you need precise control:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getInventory(warehouseId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife({
    revalidate: 300,    // 5 minutes
    expire: 600,        // 10 minutes
    stale: 3600,        // 1 hour
  });

  return await inventoryApi.getStock(warehouseId);
}

The configuration accepts seconds as numbers. The example caches inventory for 5 minutes, expires it after 10 minutes, and allows the browser to use stale data for 1 hour during navigation.

Pairing cacheLife() with cacheTag() enables on-demand invalidation:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('products', `product-${id}`);

  return await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

When you call revalidateTag('products') from a Server Action, Next.js invalidates all cache entries tagged with products. The next request for any product executes the function and generates a fresh cache entry.

Migration Patterns: Converting Legacy Caching to use cache

Migrating from Next.js 15 caching requires three steps: remove unstable_cache wrappers, replace fetch cache options, and add explicit use cache directives.

Step 1: Remove unstable_cache wrappers

Old pattern with unstable_cache:

import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

const getCachedUser = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  },
  ['user'],
  { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['users'] }
);

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  return await getCachedUser(id);
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getUser(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  cacheTag('users');

  return await db.users.findUnique({ where: { id } });
}

The directive goes inside the function body. The cache key now derives automatically from the function identity and arguments. You do not specify key parts manually.

Step 2: Replace fetch cache options

Old pattern with fetch options:

export async function getProducts() {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['products'] }
  });
  return response.json();
}

New pattern with use cache:

import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');
  cacheTag('products');

  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products');
  return response.json();
}

The fetch call no longer carries cache options. The use cache directive controls caching for the entire function, including the fetch call and any subsequent processing.

Content image showing migration from old caching patterns to use cache

Step 3: Add explicit directives to previously implicit routes

Routes that relied on implicit static optimization need explicit use cache directives. If a page component performs data fetching that should cache, add the directive:

import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');

  const { id } = await params;
  const product = await db.products.findUnique({ where: { id } });

  return <div>{product.name}</div>;
}

The migration flow moves all cache control to the function level. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply, not in build output or framework internals.

Migration flow from old caching patterns to use cache

use cache vs Data Cache vs Full Route Cache: Understanding the Cache Hierarchy

Next.js 16 maintains three cache layers: function-level cache (via use cache), prerendered HTML, and browser cache. Each serves a different purpose in the request lifecycle.

Function-level cache stores RSC payloads for individual functions and components. When you mark a function with use cache, Next.js caches its serialized return value. This cache applies during rendering. If a component calls a cached function multiple times in a single request, the framework returns the cached result after the first call.

Prerendered HTML stores complete pages generated at build time or during incremental static regeneration. When Next.js prerenders a page, it executes all cached functions, generates the RSC payload, renders HTML, and writes the HTML to disk. Subsequent requests serve the HTML directly without executing Server Components. The cacheLife expire window controls when the HTML becomes stale and triggers a background revalidation.

Browser cache stores RSC payloads the client receives during navigation or prefetching. When a user navigates to a new page, Next.js sends the RSC payload. The browser caches this payload according to the cacheLife stale window. During that window, navigating back to the page uses the cached payload without a server request.

Cache hierarchy showing function-level, HTML, and browser caches

These layers work together. A request hits the browser cache first. If the cached payload is stale, the browser requests from the server. The server checks for prerendered HTML. If the HTML is stale or missing, Next.js executes the page component. The component calls cached functions, which check the function-level cache. If a function's cached result is stale, the framework executes the function and updates the cache.

The distinction matters when you configure cacheLife. Setting revalidate to 5 minutes means the function-level cache refreshes every 5 minutes. Setting expire to 10 minutes means the prerendered HTML becomes invalid after 10 minutes. Setting stale to 1 hour means the browser uses its cached payload for 1 hour without checking the server.

Cache layer Storage location Invalidation trigger Controlled by
Function-level In-memory or remote handler revalidate window or revalidateTag() cacheLife() revalidate
Prerendered HTML Disk or platform storage expire window or deployment cacheLife() expire
Browser Client memory stale window or user action cacheLife() stale

The default cache handler stores function-level entries in memory per instance. This works for small apps but does not share cache across instances. For apps with multiple servers or serverless functions, use use cache: remote to store entries in a shared handler. The remote handler requires a network roundtrip for each cache hit, so it only pays off when the hit rate is high and the cached operation is expensive.

Production Gotchas: Cache Storage, Edge Runtime, and Common Mistakes

Production environments introduce cache storage constraints, edge runtime limitations, and developer mistakes that do not surface in local development.

Cache storage defaults to ephemeral in-memory per instance. When you deploy to a platform like Vercel, each serverless function instance maintains its own cache. Cache entries do not persist across cold starts. If an instance scales down and later scales up, the new instance starts with an empty cache. This differs from development, where next dev maintains a single long-running process with a persistent in-memory cache.

For durable shared caching, configure a cache handler in next.config.ts:

const nextConfig = {
  cacheHandlers: {
    default: {
      handler: './cache-handler.js',
    },
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

The cache handler must implement the Next.js cache handler interface. The official Redis handler provides a reference implementation. Using a remote cache introduces latency; each cache hit requires a network roundtrip to the cache store. Profile your cache hit rate before migrating. If the hit rate is low, the network overhead exceeds the benefit.

Edge runtime does not support all cache operations. Functions deployed to the edge can use use cache, but they cannot write to a durable cache handler that requires a persistent connection. The edge runtime allows only stateless HTTP requests. If your cached function must run at the edge, limit cache storage to the edge instance's memory. Cache entries do not persist across edge locations or instance restarts.

Common mistakes include caching non-serializable values, accessing runtime APIs inside cached functions, and misunderstanding cache key derivation.

Attempting to cache a class instance fails at runtime:

// This crashes when Next.js tries to serialize the cache entry
export async function getUserService(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  return new UserService(id);
}

The framework can only serialize plain objects, arrays, primitives, and React elements. Extract the data from the class instance and cache the data:

export async function getUserData(id: string) {
  'use cache';
  const service = new UserService(id);
  return await service.getData();
}

Accessing cookies() inside a cached function throws an error:

// This crashes because cookies() is a runtime API
export async function getSessionUser() {
  'use cache';
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session');
  return await db.sessions.findUnique({ where: { id: sessionId.value } });
}

Runtime APIs provide request-specific data. Caching request-specific data breaks the cache model. Move the runtime API call to a parent component and pass the value as an argument:

export async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const sessionId = cookieStore.get('session')?.value;

  if (!sessionId) {
    return <div>Not logged in</div>;
  }

  const user = await getCachedUser(sessionId);
  return <div>Hello {user.name}</div>;
}

async function getCachedUser(sessionId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('minutes');

  const session = await db.sessions.findUnique({ 
    where: { id: sessionId },
    include: { user: true }
  });

  return session?.user;
}

The cached function receives sessionId as an argument. Different session IDs produce different cache entries. The cache key includes the session ID, so each user gets their own cached entry.

Production flow showing cache handler, edge limitations, and error paths

Cache key derivation includes function identity, arguments, and captured closures. If a closure captures a value from a parent scope, that value becomes part of the key. This can produce unintended cache misses if the captured value changes frequently:

export default async function ProductList({ category }: { category: string }) {
  const baseUrl = process.env.API_URL;

  // The cache key includes both category and baseUrl
  async function fetchProducts() {
    'use cache';
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/products?category=${category}`);
    return response.json();
  }

  return <div>{await fetchProducts()}</div>;
}

If API_URL changes between deployments, the cache key changes and all entries become invalid. For stable cache keys, pass environment variables as arguments or read them inside the cached function without capturing them from closures.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should you use use cache: remote instead of the default in-memory cache?

Use use cache: remote when your app runs on multiple serverless instances or containers and the cached operation is expensive enough to justify a network roundtrip. The remote cache shares entries across instances, but each cache hit requires fetching from the remote store. Profile your cache hit rate first; if it is below 80%, the network overhead likely exceeds the benefit.

Can you cache Server Actions with use cache?

Server Actions cannot use use cache directly because they are not idempotent operations; they mutate state rather than fetch data. You can pass Server Actions through cached components to Client Components without invoking them inside the cacheable function. The cached component treats the action as a serializable prop.

What happens when you call revalidateTag() with a tag that does not exist?

Calling revalidateTag() with a non-existent tag succeeds silently without invalidating anything. The framework does not track which tags exist; it only invalidates cache entries that match the tag. If no entries match, the call has no effect. This makes tag-based invalidation safe to call speculatively.

How does Next.js handle cache entries when you redeploy your app?

A new deployment generates a new build ID, which becomes part of the cache key for all use cache entries. When the build ID changes, all previous cache entries become inaccessible. This applies to both in-memory and remote caches. The new deployment starts with an empty cache, even if you use a durable cache handler.

Can you use use cache in Client Components?

Client Components cannot use use cache because they run in the browser, which has no server-side cache. The directive only works in Server Components and server-side async functions. If you need to cache data in a Client Component, fetch it in a Server Component, cache the Server Component with use cache, and pass the data as props.

Conclusion: Building a Mental Model for Next.js 16 Caching

The mental model for Next.js 16 caching reduces to three principles: mark what you cache, state when it expires, name it for invalidation. Every cache decision is explicit. No framework heuristics infer whether a route should cache. No fetch calls carry hidden cache options. No compiler analysis determines static versus dynamic rendering.

Add use cache to functions that fetch data or render UI. Call cacheLife() to set expiration windows. Call cacheTag() to enable on-demand invalidation. The compiler generates cache keys from function identity, arguments, and captured closures. Arguments and return values must be serializable. Runtime APIs like cookies() cannot be called inside cached functions.

Migration from Next.js 15 requires removing unstable_cache wrappers, replacing fetch cache options, and adding explicit directives. Production deployments need cache handler configuration for durable shared caching. Edge deployments limit cache to in-memory per instance. Cache entries do not persist across deployments because the build ID becomes part of the cache key.

The result is a caching model where developers control every aspect. You see caching decisions in the code where they apply. You reason about cache behavior the same way everywhere: functions, components, routes. You configure freshness requirements once, at the function level, rather than in multiple places with conflicting options. For teams managing complex data dependencies, this clarity eliminates an entire class of production bugs.

articles.title: I made $0 from my side project for 8 months. Then one furious email at 2am changed everything.
articles.description: For eight months, the most-visited tab in my browser was a Stripe dashboard that said $0.00.  I'd...
articles.body_html:
For eight months, the most-visited tab in my browser was a Stripe dashboard that said $0.00.

I'd open it first thing in the morning, the way other people check the weather. Refresh. $0.00. Refresh again, because maybe it hadn't loaded. $0.00. Then I'd close it, open my editor, and go do the thing I was sure would finally move that number: ship another feature.

I shipped a lot of features. Dark mode. A second onboarding flow because I didn't like the first. CSV export nobody asked for. A settings page with toggles for things that didn't need toggling. I posted on launch-day forums. I rewrote the landing page headline four times. I A/B tested a button color like the button color was the problem.

Eight months. Roughly thirty features. Exactly zero dollars.

And then, in a single week, it stopped being zero — not because of a feature, a growth hack, or a headline. Because of one furious email at 2am. I want to tell you exactly what that email changed, because it rewired how I think about building anything, and it's the opposite of every "just ship more" post you've ever scrolled past.

The thing I was actually doing for eight months

Here's the uncomfortable reframe, and it took me far too long to see it.

For eight months, I was producing output. A feature is output. A settings toggle is output. A fourth headline is output. Every one of those thirty things was a real, deployed, working piece of software that existed because I typed it into being.

And output — the typing, the scaffolding, the "make a thing that exists" — is the part that got free. I was writing most of that code with an AI by then, shipping faster than I ever had in my life. I could produce a polished feature in an afternoon. I was a one-person feature factory running at full tilt.

$0.00 is exactly what a feature factory running at full tilt is worth, if that's all it is.

Because the number on the dashboard was never waiting on another feature. I kept treating $0 as a production problem — not enough shipped, not polished enough, not enough toggles — when it was never a production problem at all. The hard part of a product was never the code, and it definitely isn't the code anymore. The hard part is a single stranger caring enough to depend on the thing, come back to it, and be genuinely hurt when it breaks. I had compressed the easy 20% — the building — to almost nothing, and spent eight months doing more and more of it, while the impossible 80% sat there untouched.

I wasn't building a business. I was building a very productive graveyard, one tombstone a week.

What the 2am email actually was

I had a free trial. A handful of people had started one over those months — I'd watch them poke around for ten minutes and vanish. Output going out, nobody depending on it. Fine. Zero.

Then one trial user did something none of the others had: they used it. For real. Put their actual work in it, came back the next day, and the day after. One stranger, finally leaning their weight on the thing I'd made.

And the thing I'd made had a bug I'd shipped months earlier and never noticed, because noticing it required someone to actually depend on it. I had a write path that acknowledged the request before it had actually persisted the row. In the demo, in my tests, on my machine — flawless.
