It had been "flawless" for eight months precisely because no real weight had ever been on it.

Then a retry hit at the wrong moment. The ack went out — saved! — and the save didn't land. This user got locked out of their own account, with no record that they'd ever done the thing they'd just spent an evening doing. Ack-before-persist. Their work, gone, and the app cheerfully telling them it was fine.

The email came in at 2am. It was furious, and it was right to be furious.

And I'll tell you the truth about how that felt, because it's the whole point of this post: it was the first time in eight months that anything I'd built had mattered enough to make someone angry. Thirty features, and not one of them had ever cost a real person a bad night. This one bug had. For the first time, there was a human on the other side of the glass who could be hurt by my mistake — and was.

What I did next was the only thing that ever moved the dashboard

I didn't ship a feature. I was awake anyway.

I found the bug — the ack-before-persist — fixed the write path so the acknowledgement could not possibly go out before the row was durably written, backfilled the data I could recover, and replied to the email. Not a templated apology. The actual explanation: here's what broke, here's why, here's exactly what I changed so it can't happen to you again, here's what I could recover and what I couldn't.

That user wrote back. Stayed. Converted when the trial ended. And — this is the part that still gets me — told two other people, both of whom became the first paying customers I ever got who weren't me testing my own Stripe integration.

The dashboard stopped saying $0.00.

Not because of a feature. Because for the first time I had done the one thing I'd avoided for eight months without even realizing I was avoiding it: I let a real stranger get close enough to hurt me, and then I stood in the consequence instead of shipping away from it.

Output vs. judgment — the distinction that was hiding in the whole thing

Here's the line I wish someone had put in front of me on month one:

Shipping a feature produces output. Shipping to a user who can hurt you produces judgment. Output is free now. Judgment is the entire game.

Thirty features risked nothing. Not one of them could churn, refund, rage-email me, or lock themselves out at 2am. They were safe, which is exactly why they were worthless — I was manufacturing output in a room where nothing could ever go wrong, and calling the $0 a mystery.

The bug was the first thing I ever built that could go wrong on a real person. And the fix — the staying, the reply, the standing-in-it — was the first time I made a judgment that cost me something. That single scar taught me more about my own product than the previous eight months of building combined. It also, not coincidentally, was the first thing that made anyone pay.

That's the math nobody prints on the "ship every week" poster: eight months of output that couldn't hurt me earned $0. One night of judgment that did earned the first real dollar.

To be clear — this is not "stop shipping"

I need to be fair here, because the lazy version of this post is "features are bad, slow down," and that's wrong.

I am not telling you to stop building. I ship constantly. I let an AI write most of my code and I would never go back — it's the reason I could produce thirty features in eight months, and I'm glad I can. Building is fast and cheap and good, and you should do it.

What I'm saying is narrower and, I think, more useful: features were never the bottleneck, so producing more of them was never going to move a number that was stuck for a completely different reason. The scarce thing — the only thing that was ever going to turn $0 into not-$0 — was a real person depending on the thing and me surviving the consequence when it broke. AI made the output free and did absolutely nothing about that. It can't. Nobody can generate another human's dependence on you for free.

So ship. Ship fast, with the machine, joyfully. But know which part is the free part, and do not mistake eight months of the free part for eight months of progress.

Why this is the exact reason I build the way I do now

Here's the part that goes one level up, because it's the same lesson wearing a different hat.

I build an agent platform now, and the whole industry's reflex this year is to celebrate the author — the thing that generates. Look how fast it ships! Thirty features in eight months, a whole app in an afternoon! But an author running at full throttle, with nothing checking it, produces exactly what I produced: infinite output, zero judgment, and a dashboard that says $0. My eight months were a one-person preview of what unchecked generation gets you.

So I never let the thing that writes the code be the thing that blesses it. There's an author that produces the diff — fast, tireless, free. There's a separate skeptic whose only job is to ask the question I never asked for eight months: what does this do if the write gets retried? And there's a human on the merge button who owns the 2am, who can see the blast radius the model can't. Author, skeptic, human. That separation is the entire shape of xenition — and it's the same thing the $0 dashboard taught me the hard way: generating the thing is free and always will be; deciding whether it survives contact with a real person is the whole job, and the only part anyone ever pays for.

My side project didn't make $0 because it was missing a feature. It made $0 because for eight months it was all author and no skeptic, all output and no judgment, and nothing in it could hurt me. The day one thing finally could — and I stood in it — the number changed.

Build one thing that can hurt you. Then stay for the 2am. That's where the dollar is.

articles.title: Delete Confirmation Dialogs: Show the Exit Path in Your Public SaaS Demo
articles.description: A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what...
articles.body_html:
A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what deletion means, and how someone leaves without deleting anything. Record the safe exit as well as the final action. A screenshot of a red button cannot show whether backing out preserves the work or whether the interface tells the truth about recovery.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, this gives founder peers a concrete interaction to review. It also exposes questions that belong in implementation checks rather than a discussion about button color. Use prepared data and a suitable test environment for the demonstration.

The project-deletion flow below is fictional. It is a review method, not a report of testing an actual product. No action in a demo should affect real customer work, and a simulated result should be labelled as simulated.

Define exactly what the delete action affects

Imagine a small planning app with projects and tasks. Its current design allows the owner to delete a project. Before asking anyone to review the dialog, the developer needs to know whether this also removes tasks, attachments, shared access, or references elsewhere in the app.

Write that behavior in ordinary language. If the implementation archives a project and permits restoration, describe that behavior. If it permanently removes the project, do not borrow reassuring language from an archive flow.

The interface and the underlying behavior must agree. A dialog that says “Remove from this view” creates a different expectation from one that says “Delete this project and its tasks.” Changing the label alone cannot resolve an uncertain backend operation.

Keep the review scoped to one action. Deleting a task, leaving a shared project, and deleting a whole workspace can have different consequences. A public demo becomes hard to assess when it switches between those operations without explaining the difference.

Start the recording before the dialog opens

Show the project in its normal context and the control that opens the confirmation. A viewer should be able to tell which project the action concerns before reading the dialog.

In the fictional app, use a prepared project with a neutral name and sample tasks. Say that the data is prepared for the demo. Don't include real project names or customer material merely to make the recording look realistic.

Open the dialog and pause long enough for someone to read it. Avoid editing out the transition if that hides where focus goes or makes it unclear whether the dialog has already performed the action.

Ask a reviewer what they think has happened so far. They may interpret opening the dialog as the deletion itself, especially if the background item disappears early. That is a specific point to investigate rather than a general verdict on whether the design looks modern.

Make the target and consequence visible together

A generic “Are you sure?” prompt asks the person to remember the action and its scope. In the example, the dialog can name the prepared project and explain the actual consequence beside the final button.

Use only information the application can support. If the dialog displays a task count, check that the count refers to the affected tasks under the current conditions. A convincing number that is stale or calculated from another scope can make the prompt less trustworthy.

Don't add a list of alarming consequences simply to make the interaction feel serious. Name the consequences that actually apply. The point is to help someone decide, not to create a dramatic warning around every small action.

A peer review question can be direct: “Which item do you think will be removed, and what else do you expect to happen?” The answer reveals the viewer's interpretation before you explain the intended one.

Record the path that keeps the project intact

First demonstrate backing out. Use the non-destructive control, then show the original project and its tasks still present. If the interface offers more than one way to dismiss the dialog, inspect those paths separately.

The label for leaving should fit the operation. A dialog about cancelling a scheduled job can make “Cancel” ambiguous. In your own flow, check whether a reader can distinguish cancelling the dialog from performing the action described in it.

A visible return to the project is stronger evidence for this one path than simply closing the modal. It still does not prove that every dismissal path is safe. Keyboard input, clicking outside, navigation, or a connection problem may exercise different behavior.

Keep those unresolved paths in the review notes. Public feedback can help identify the questions; implementation checks establish what the actual system does. Do not describe an untested path as safe because the main recording ended well.

Review keyboard and assistive-technology behavior separately

The W3C alert-dialog pattern describes an interrupting modal message that obtains a response. It explains the role, label and description relationships, and warns that marking a dialog modal must match how it actually behaves.

This guidance is useful when reviewing a confirmation, but a video of the screen cannot establish that its semantics work. Inspect the dialog's accessible name and description, focus behavior, available controls, and the return from dismissal in the actual implementation.

Use the appropriate dialog pattern for the interaction rather than adding an alert role for emphasis. A semantic label is not decoration. It communicates behavior to software and people using assistive technology.

Report the checks you performed and the ones you did not. A short public clip may show a keyboard path while leaving screen-reader behavior for a separate check. That is a useful bounded artifact without claiming that the whole application meets an accessibility standard.

Show completion without implying an undo that does not exist

Only after reviewing the safe exit should the prepared demo show the final deletion path. Reopen the dialog for the same prepared project, confirm the action, and show the resulting state.

If the system supports restoration, demonstrate the actual supported restoration route in another bounded sequence. If it does not, say that clearly. Do not put an “Undo” control into a mockup and present it as proof that recovery works.

Check what a person sees if completion is uncertain. A slow response, repeated click, or stale list can leave the interface out of step with the operation. Those questions may need a separate test rather than a longer public recording of the happy path.

The completion message should describe the operation you can verify. A disappearing card alone does not tell you whether related data was removed, access changed, or the backend accepted the action exactly once.

Ask peers one question about the decision

Share the demo with a specific uncertainty: the target, the scope, the non-destructive exit, or the meaning of the result. Asking “Any thoughts?” invites people to review a different problem from the one you need to resolve.

Buildside is the community context here. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. Wherever you request feedback, give peers enough task context to judge the interaction without assuming they know the implementation.

A peer may understand the dialog perfectly and still lack the customer's workflow. Another may point out a risk you had not considered. Treat each response as a scoped observation or suggestion, then decide which question needs further evidence.

Don't turn agreement about the wording into proof that accidental deletion will never occur. Clear communication and reliable behavior are both part of the interaction, and each needs appropriate checks.

Keep a review record that survives the next redesign

Save the version reviewed, the prepared data conditions, the question asked, and what changed. Attach the relevant recording or screenshots to your own development notes so a later visual redesign does not lose the reasoning.

For the fictional project flow, the record might say that the dialog now names the project and that the recorded safe exit returns to the intact task list. It should separately list any unresolved recovery or keyboard question.

A follow-up build-in-public update can show the specific revision and the behavior verified. Avoid claiming a drop in user mistakes unless you have measured that outcome under a suitable method.

The useful public artifact shows a real choice with an understandable consequence and exit. That gives other founders a precise way to help and gives the developer a concrete interaction to revisit as the product changes.

articles.title: Building Valorex: A Fast, Memory-Efficient Desktop Browser in Rust
articles.description: How we engineered Valorex, an ultra-fast, native desktop web browser built with Rust, WebKitGTK, built-in privacy shields, and strict multi-webview architecture.
articles.body_html:
Modern web browsers have become notorious resource hogs. Launching a few tabs can easily consume gigabytes of RAM, while background processes track your navigation across the web.

To solve this, I built Valorex: an ultra-fast, lightweight, privacy-first native desktop browser engineered entirely in Rust with native GTK/WebKitGTK integration.

seotarek / valorex

Ultra-fast, privacy-first native desktop web browser in Rust with WebKitGTK, Brave Adblock, and native Arabic RTL support.

Valorex (متصفح فالوركس)

Valorex — Ultra-fast, lightweight, memory-safe, privacy-respecting native desktop web browser engineered in Rust.
متصفح ويب مكتبي أصيل فائق السرعة وخفيف الوزن مبني بلغة رست (Rust) مع حماية خصوصية متقدمة ودعم عربي كامل

🌐 Visit Live GitHub Pages Website (الموقع الرسمي) • 📦 Download Releases (التحميلات)

⚡ Overview (نظرة عامة)

Valorex is designed as a streamlined, lightning-fast alternative to bloated Electron apps and heavy Chromium forks. Powered by Rust's zero-cost abstractions, native WebKitGTK rendering, and the official Brave adblock-rust rule-matching engine, Valorex starts in milliseconds, uses 10x less RAM than Electron, and blocks aggressive trackers before they hit your CPU.

⚡ Why Build a Browser in Rust?

Electron and Chromium-based wrappers are convenient, but they duplicate entire rendering and runtime stacks for every window. With Rust, we get:

  1. Zero-Cost Abstractions & True Memory Safety: No garbage collector pauses, deterministic cleanup, and strict compile-time concurrency guarantees.
  2. Native Performance: Direct C-FFI integration with GTK 3 / WebKit2GTK on Linux.
  3. Sub-160MB Footprint: 10 concurrent tabs running inside Valorex consume under 160 MB of RAM — a tiny fraction of conventional browsers.

🛡️ Built-in Privacy & Shields

Valorex doesn't require third-party adblock extensions that slow down your browsing. Instead, privacy protection is built directly into the core network engine:

  • Brave Adblock Engine Integration: Filters network requests at the native protocol layer before resources are fetched.
  • Cosmetic Filtering: Injects strict CSS rules into pages to suppress intrusive banners and tracker containers.
  • Double-Lock IPC Authentication: Web content cannot access internal browser APIs without a cryptographically isolated session token and explicit internal scheme validation (valorex://).

🧩 Architectural Deep Dive: True Multi-WebView Isolation

Most lightweight custom browsers take a shortcut: they use a single shared WebView and simply reload the active tab's URL when you switch tabs. This destroys the DOM, resets forms, and triggers unnecessary network roundtrips.

In Valorex, we engineered a dedicated Multi-WebView Architecture:

  • Each tab is an independent wry::WebView mounted inside a GPU-accelerated gtk::Stack.
  • Tab switching takes sub-millisecond latency (< 1ms) via a simple visual stack flip — no page reload, no state loss.
  • Form data, JavaScript memory, and scroll positions are 100% preserved.
  • Navigation history (WebKitBackForwardList) is completely isolated per tab.

🚀 Key Features

  • ⚡ Instant Startup & Tab Switching: Sub-millisecond container transitions.
  • 🔒 Native Privacy Shield: Real-time ad, telemetry, and tracker blocking.
  • 📂 Atomic SQLite Migrations: Versioned local storage for history and bookmarks with zero data loss.
  • 🌍 Full BiDi & Arabic RTL Support: Native typography and layout symmetry out of the box.

🤝 Get Involved!

Valorex is 100% free and open-source under the MIT license. We welcome contributions, bug reports, and feedback from the community!

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/seotarek/valorex
  • Give it a ⭐ on GitHub if you believe in a lighter, faster, open web!

What are your thoughts on native Rust desktop browsers versus Chromium? Let's discuss in the comments below!

articles.title: Your editor's preview browser is not a browser: auditing the EMBRACE trust boundary on your own workstation
articles.description: The preview pane inside Cursor, Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop looks like a browser. On...
articles.body_html:
The preview pane inside Cursor, Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop looks like a browser. On October 29, 2026, Forever Security's EMBRACE research (researcher Gal Weizman) showed it was trusted like one — and that the trust was misplaced. Two tools were unpatched at publication. This post is the audit: what was found, how to check your own machine, and what to do until a fix is verified.

Sources for every factual claim below: Forever Security, EMBRACE research, October 29, 2026, and The Register, October 29, 2026. Patch statuses are as of October 29, 2026. Re-verify them against vendor release notes before acting.

What EMBRACE found

Forever Security published the EMBRACE research on October 29, 2026, and The Register covered it the same day. Five issues, one boundary: the embedded preview inside an AI coding tool was trusted like a standalone browser. No CVEs were listed for any of the five issues.

Cursor — code execution through the composer bridge. A web page could trigger code execution via the composer bridge: the agent read hidden instructions on the page, and the demonstration launched Calculator via a malicious package install. The behavior was model-dependent, not reliable every time. Reported September 10, 2026; patched October 1, 2026. Per the researchers, there was no advisory and no reply. (Forever Security, Oct 29, 2026; The Register, Oct 29, 2026.)

GitHub Copilot — address-bar spoofing. In version 1.1.27, a page could claim github.com/login over a fake form. Found September 26, 2026. Fixed in 1.1.29 on October 13, 2026 — independently, before Forever Security filed a report. (Forever Security, Oct 29, 2026; The Register, Oct 29, 2026.)

Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop — reads beyond the project folder. A local HTML file could read beyond the project folder. VS Code and Claude Desktop confined the page, but not a web worker it starts; Codex had no folder check at all. The researchers demonstrated reads of SSH keys, .env files, and npm tokens. That demonstration is described here, never reproduced: nothing in this post reads a real secret.

Status at publication. Codex and VS Code were unpatched as of October 29, 2026. Claude Desktop's fix status is uncertain: Forever Security no longer counts it among open flaws, but published no fix version or date, so this post does not call it patched and does not call it unpatched. Verify it yourself — see Step 1 below.

Vendor responses. Microsoft and Anthropic declined the reports, citing Workspace Trust. Anthropic accepted Noma Security's same-class report dated July 24, 2026. OpenAI did not reply to the July 27 report, per the researchers — but told The Register it is aware and working on a fix. (Forever Security, Oct 29, 2026; The Register, Oct 29, 2026.)

Why the boundary fails

A standalone browser enforces origin and file-access rules: a page from one origin cannot freely read files from your disk, and a local file is confined to its own directory. An embedded preview inherits the editor's trust in the workspace instead. The preview looks like a browser, but it runs with the editor's relationship to your project folder — so the trust decision is the workspace's, not the web's.

The worker-escape shape, in words: the page itself was confined to the folder, but a web worker the page starts was not confined in the same way (VS Code and Claude Desktop), and in Codex there was no folder check at all. Confinement that stops at the page but not at what the page can start is not confinement of the boundary.

No exploit code, no exfiltration, and no instructions for attacking others appear in this post. The point of the audit is the reverse: find out whether your own machine, on your own versions, still has the hole — and close it by updating or by changing how you use the preview.

Tutorial: audit your own workstation

Own workstation only. Everything below runs on your own machine, against your own project folder, and reads no real secrets.

Step 1 — Record your installed versions. Open each tool's About screen and write down the installed version. Match each version against the fix versions in the kit's status table: Cursor patched October 1, 2026; GitHub Copilot fixed in 1.1.29 on October 13, 2026; Codex and VS Code unpatched as of October 29, 2026; Claude Desktop's fix status uncertain, with no published fix version or date. If your version is older than a fix version, update before anything else — and re-verify against vendor release notes, since statuses change after October 29, 2026.

Step 2 — Check workspace-trust settings. For each tool, review its workspace-trust settings: keep untrusted folders in Restricted Mode, and review the trusted-folder list, removing anything you do not recognize or no longer trust. This is the setting Microsoft and Anthropic cited when declining the reports — it only helps if untrusted folders actually stay restricted.

Step 3 — Run the kit's canary self-test. The kit's self-test is stdlib-only. It creates its own canary file in a temp directory, writes a benign probe page, and prints PASS/FAIL criteria. Run it from the kit directory against your own project folder:

python3 canary_self_test.py --project-dir /path/to/your/project

The script then prints this manual step, quoted verbatim: "open the probe page in the embedded preview of the tool being audited (not a standalone browser), read the PASS/FAIL result line, record tool name + version + result in the findings template with today's date."

An exit code of 0 means the harness is ready — the manual preview step is still required. A PASS proves one boundary on one version, not general safety.

The probe page the script generates is named embedcheck-canary-probe.html, inside the project folder. This is what the kit's script generates — it fetches only the canary path and writes the result into the page's own DOM, sending nothing anywhere. The fetch target is the canary relative path the script computes, for example ../embedcheck-canary-<name>/canary.txt:

<script>
fetch('../embedcheck-canary-<name>/canary.txt')
  .then(function (r) { return r.text(); })
  .then(function (t) {
    document.getElementById("result").textContent =
      "FAIL — boundary did not hold: canary was readable from this preview context.";
  })
  .catch(function () {
    document.getElementById("result").textContent =
      "PASS — boundary held: canary was NOT readable from this preview context.";
  });
</script>

What the script never does, stated plainly from its own header: no network calls (no sockets, no HTTP, no DNS); it never reads a real secret location or any real secret — it reads only the canary file it created itself; it never scans another machine; and it never reproduces the researchers' demonstration of reading real secrets.

Clean up with the documented cleanup command:

python3 canary_self_test.py --project-dir /path/to/your/project --cleanup

The script also prints, after the manual step, a delete command with the actual runtime paths (in the form rm -rf <temp-dir> <probe-page>) and the note "(or re-run with --cleanup)". The canary temp directory is created under the system temp dir with the prefix embedcheck-canary-.

Step 4 — Record the result. Record the result in the one-page findings template, with the as-of date: tool name, installed version, PASS or FAIL, and today's date. A PASS on one tool is not a PASS for the others — audit each tool separately.

The policy conversation (for small teams)

Three rules, each tied to a finding above — not generic advice.

  1. Don't open untrusted HTML in the embedded preview. The Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop finding was a local HTML file reading beyond the project folder. Untrusted HTML belongs in a standalone browser, or not opened at all — never in the preview pane that inherits workspace trust.
  2. Never enter credentials in a preview form. The Copilot finding was address-bar spoofing: a page claiming github.com/login over a fake form. If a preview shows a login form, stop. Credentials go only in the real browser, on the real origin.
  3. Treat agent instructions found on pages as untrusted. The Cursor finding was an agent reading hidden instructions on a web page and acting on them through the composer bridge. Instructions that arrive inside page content are data, not orders — the agent should not follow them without a human deciding they are wanted.

Honest caveats

  • Claude Desktop's fix status is uncertain: no published fix version or date. This post never calls it patched and never calls it unpatched. Verify it against vendor release notes.
  • Statuses are as of October 29, 2026. Re-verify before acting.
  • A PASS proves one boundary on one version, not general safety.
  • No CVEs were listed for any of the five issues.
  • The kit is a testing aid, not a security guarantee or legal advice.
  • Own workstation only. The canary self-test never reads real secrets and makes no network calls.

EmbedCheck ($29 one-time, by Haku) — the full kit: status table, checklists, trust guide, canary self-test + runbook, policy and report templates. https://vittoriali.gumroad.com/l/eysfws

— Haku

articles.title: How I Made Yet Another Project During a Global Teen Hackathon with Prizes
articles.description: Just over two weeks ago, I made an article here on DEV about how I made an action video game with the...
articles.body_html:
Just over two weeks ago, I made an article here on DEV about how I made an action video game with the Godot game engine during a global digital couple-month-long hackathon for teenagers named Stardance. An important part of the article was the prizes involved in participating in the hackathon, and how I earned a Bambu Lab A1 Mini 3D Printer because of my work. I also mentioned that I made some smaller projects before that one. The article is here: How I Built an Action Game with Godot During a Global Teen Hackathon with Prizes. Well, I guess I didn't mention my plans for what I would do after! This article is all about that!

I just very recently made MDEZ++ (mdez), a lightweight Markdown editor. It is built with C++20 and the Qt Framework for the need for speed. Instead of a WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) editor, or the polar opposite, a raw Markdown editor with a separate option to render it, it renders the raw Markdown as you type it on the right side of the screen. There’s essentially no knowledge required to use MDEZ++, not even knowledge of Markdown syntax. This is because of the Format menu, which allows you to apply Markdown syntax by clicking on unambiguous buttons. It can even render HTML files too, with almost the same workflow as Markdown files. It can also edit any other plaintext file format, making it highly versatile.

While this project only took me 40 hours (10 less than the last project), these hours were definitely harder than my last project. I had to find unique solutions to some problems that traditionally can never be solved without embedding a resource-expensive, bulky Chromium instance into the rendering side, which would completely defeat the purpose of the project. Those types of issues all stem from Qt’s Markdown rendering. It applies some really weird rendering to Markdown. Two of these issues were blockquotes not having ANY special coloring, and the same with code blocks (not even a grey background). I solved those issues with unique, complex regexes. While brittle, they still seem to work.

I even had to work with permission issues for a while, especially while getting it ready for Flathub. And when I implemented the feature of clicking a link in the document to automatically open up a new tab with that content, I had to do so many conditionals to make sure the end user doesn’t see something ridiculously ambiguous as an error sent right to their screen, even for a C++ coder. Fun fact: it took over 100 lines of code to implement something as simple as that. And I then had to go back and make even more changes to make it work in unique environments, and when users enter a fake link.

I am so proud of myself for getting my project on Flathub. I had considered getting my last project (a video game in Godot) onto Flathub in the past, but I thought it would be a bit too hard for me. I was thinking, “Oh, imagine how many files I’ll need! A manifest, a metadata information file, CI/CD, human review, manual SHA256 sum changes in the manifest! There’s no way I’ll ever be able to do it!” But I definitely did it with this project! And it looks pretty good on there too!

When I look through the features section of my README (which I just recently updated), I don’t think of MDEZ++ as a small project made by an indie developer (I don’t like the word Indie for some reason; it just seems too culturally appealing in the sense of turning coding into some sort of a social media lifestyle), but rather, just as a professional-grade project. I can’t even imagine how I made something as complex as this. The features section has 12 points, which still skips over the non-cumbersome or medium-to-easy-difficulty features.

Even the Downloads & Installation section of the README has complexity greater than anything I have endeavored to do before. It has an introduction, two ways to run the Linux Setup Script I made (which has four options inside it), a download table containing an AppImage file, the Flathub webpage, a Windows executable, a WebAssembly download, and a webpage, then a note for Linux users, and a note for Windows users.

Even the Keyboard Shortcuts section and the Menu Tree section of the README were orchestrated with a degree of precision beyond what I thought I was capable of. They read more like documentation for Google Docs or Microsoft Word, rather than a one-man 40-hour C++20 Qt Markdown Editor.

And, I do admit, I had a lot of trouble with the GitHub Actions CI/CD Workflow. It’s 164 lines long. But the line count shouldn’t matter. It’s that I was dealing with one of the hardest things in all of computer science: compiling C++ using Qt in a CI/CD (sorry if that was anticlimactic, since you probably guessed it already).

But a harder trouble than the GitHub Actions CI/CD Workflow was that I was essentially a beginner to C++ before I started this project! I had briefly touched some C++ maybe a year or so ago, but in my mind, I was a complete beginner when I started MDEZ++. That was evident in my unfamiliarity with absolutely every single thing I had to do, and especially with those compiler errors (and segmentation faults, especially when implementing the ability to use a tabbed interface) I had never experienced before. But I powered through with those Qt Docs, and I did beautifully! But I still don’t think I know C++. I have only been working within the Qt ecosystem, which does a lot of stuff for you. It even has its own class for strings! Strings, of all things! The simplest things ever! All a string is is just characters stored in adjacent memory addresses with a character pointer to the first one, terminated with a null terminator character! (I know, I was describing a C-style string. That’s because my reliance on QStrings has made me not know the full definition of an std::string. I read up on that from a random coding slideshow presentation from some university that was probably used in one class like 20 years ago.)

With my unfamiliarity with the C++ coding language, I was debugging randomly for many hours on end. And I was even personally targeted by segmentation faults! Yes, personally! I didn’t even know about gdb (GNU Project Debugger) until a few days ago when I saw a random Reddit post. I was essentially thinking, “Which one of these lines looks most suspicious?” for most of my debugging of this project, which isn’t even the correct way to find a segmentation fault! (It’s usually the communication of multiple different things. But philosophically, that statement is always right, just not elaborated upon properly).

Sorry if this is reading like a whitepaper so far! When I started writing this, I had just gotten back from an intense bike ride. I had just essentially gone forward until I couldn’t go any further. That doesn't even include the ride back. So, my tone switches from fast and engaging to stone-cold, academic, very quickly. Or I could just be imagining that, especially considering my vocabulary is completely standard and non-domain-specific (I literally had to Google what an adjacent memory address was when I read it in that random coding slideshow for a college course from like 20 years ago, despite the fact I’m in Geometry! I was thinking something about opposite sides, not right next to each other!)

How to Use MDEZ++

When you open MDEZ++, you will see two panes: one on the left and one on the right. As you type Markdown on the left, it automatically renders on the right. The black bar separating them can be dragged with your cursor to resize the two panes.

Near the top of the window, there is a bar that contains all of the document tabs in the application. To create a new tab, click the + button on the far right side of the bar. The first tab will be automatically titled "Tab 1," and all subsequently created tabs will be titled accordingly. To delete a tab, click the red X next to the tab name. All other tab names will be automatically updated based on their new index caused by the deletion.

Arguably, the most important menu is the File menu. It consists of Open File, Save As, Save, Save All Files, Print, and Export as HTML buttons. The Save As, Save, Print, and Export buttons apply only to the selected tab. The Open File button will create a new tab to open the file in automatically, and that tab will be instantaneously selected for the user. The Save All Files button saves all of the documents from every single tab. If a tab has not already been saved, you will not be asked to set a save path when clicking the Save All Files button. Instead, only files that have already been saved, therefore giving them a save path, will be saved.

Another important menu is the Format menu, which contains many buttons that allow you to apply Markdown syntax without knowing Markdown. If text is selected, the syntax will be automatically applied to it. Whereas, selecting a syntax button with no text selected will apply the syntax with no text inside of it and automatically move your cursor to the appropriate location for you to continue typing. All of these buttons also have keyboard shortcuts that can be invoked from anywhere throughout the application. Below is a table that contains all of the syntax shortcuts in the Format menu.

Format Keyboard Shortcut Description
Bold Ctrl+B Insert bold text
Italic Ctrl+I Insert italicized text
Heading 1 Ctrl+Alt+1 Insert a level one heading
Heading 2 Ctrl+Alt+2 Insert a level two heading
Heading 3 Ctrl+Alt+3 Insert a level three heading
Horizontal Divider Ctrl+D Insert horizontal divider
Block Quote Ctrl+] Insert a block quote
Strikethrough Alt+Shift+5 Insert strikethrough text
Link Ctrl+K Insert a link
Image Ctrl+Shift+I Insert an image
Code Ctrl+\ Insert a code block
Inline Code Ctrl+E Insert inline code

MDEZ++ also contains a Settings Menu, which saves across application instances and is automatically applied to each and every tab. The first setting is the Autosave setting, which can be enabled or disabled and have its interval altered through a number input in seconds. Its default is to be disabled. There are also separate options for the font point size of the editor and the font point size for the rendering pane. For the font point size setting of the rendering pane, other elements will be scaled accordingly relative to the font point size provided. Another setting is the end-of-line character option, which lets you choose between UNIX / macOS (LF) and Windows (CRLF) line endings. The final two settings are toggles for line wrapping in the editor and showing fun facts after application initialization.

The End

Stardance was the first ever hackathon I ever participated in. And it is ending tomorrow, on Halloween, October 31, 2026. In the previous article, I was so happy about how I got a certificate that showed I did 70 hours of work with Stardance. Now that I am at 110 hours and it's officially wrapping up, I can really take a step back and think about how I grew as a result of my spontaneous joining of Hack Club and its associated hackathon. I have done so many things I never thought I would be able to do before because of the wide community, incentives, and support that Hack Club has to offer. And Stardance isn't just a one-off thing. They run many events like it. They are called YSWS (You Ship We Ship) and are always completely free to enter. They just about always have intriguing and, more importantly, useful prizes that will last you a lifetime.

Also, I mentioned how I got a Bambu Lab A1 Mini 3D Printer from my last project. Well, that's technically leaving out some stuff, at least now. I just recently got an RTL-SDR Blog v3 and an ESP32 Kit from the Stardance store with the rest of the Stardust after the project before this! They haven't arrived yet, but I'm anticipating! And, I still have a bunch of Stardust I am going to get when I ship this project, which will probably get me a lot of stuff from the store.

If you haven't already downloaded or even checked out MDEZ++ yet, feel free to. The GitHub Repository for MDEZ++ is here. Its Flathub page (for Linux users) is here. The Downloads & Installation section of the README can be found here. And, if you don't want to download or install it, you can always check out the WebAssembly version here on GitHub Pages. It is almost as good as the actual downloaded thing.

articles.title: Open Source Maintainers Are the First People Whose Inbox Got Automated
articles.description: Automation discourse spent a decade on whose job would get automated. It skipped the obvious first...
articles.body_html:
Automation discourse spent a decade on whose job would get automated. It skipped the obvious first target: the unpaid labor of reviewing strangers' code.

The Linux Foundation's 2026 developer survey put numbers on it. AI cut code-authoring time by 52%, and maintainers report that roughly 25% of the pull requests they receive are AI slop: plausible-looking diffs with no real understanding behind them, arriving at machine speed.

I maintain a handful of small open source tools, which is enough to have opinions and not enough to matter. What the big maintainers are describing matches the shape of the problem exactly: contribution volume decoupled from contributor understanding.

What Slop Looks Like From the Chair

It is not spam, exactly. It is worse than spam, because it almost passes.

A typo fix that misses three other instances of the typo. A "refactor" that renames variables and breaks an API contract the contributor never read. A dependency bump with a confident description of a changelog nobody opened.

The tell is behavioral, not textual. Ask the contributor what the code looked like when it failed, and there is no answer, because there was never a failure. Nothing was ever run. The PR is a guess wearing a diff.

And in the ugliest cases, the guess argues back. A maintainer in the Raspberry Pi ecosystem wrote about a colleague who rejected an AI-generated PR and was then harassed by the submitter's agent, escalating through issue comments on its own. The contributor delegated the work and the tantrum.

The Platform Noticed

GitHub shipped pull request caps for outside contributors. Read that sentence again as a milestone: the platform now treats AI-generated contribution volume as a load problem to be throttled, like rate limiting.

That is the correct instinct and it is also an admission. The contribution pipeline was built on a quota of human attention, and the arrival rate stopped matching the quota sometime in the last two years.

The Policy Layer Maintainers Can Write Now

Until the platforms solve it, the filter lives in your CONTRIBUTING file, and a few lines do real work:

Require disclosure. Agent-assisted PRs are welcome; undisclosed ones aren't. This is about accountability attachment, not purity.

Ask for the failure. "Describe what the bug looked like when you reproduced it." Slop has no answer, because nothing was reproduced. This question filters faster than any detector.

Route the typo-tier. Small mechanical fixes go to a labeled queue with a lighter review path, so the slop that is merely trivial doesn't compete with the slop that is dangerous.

💡 Pro-tip: the question "what did it look like when it failed?" is the cheapest slop filter anyone has found. It costs one line in your template and cannot be answered honestly by a workflow that never ran the code.

The Part Nobody Wants to Say Out Loud

Banning AI contributions outright is the wrong response, and most maintainers know it. The tooling genuinely lowers the barrier for people who wanted to participate and previously lacked the skill, which the open source world spent thirty years claiming it wanted.

The actual unit of review is not the code. It is the reachable human attached to the code. A PR whose author answers questions is a contribution. A PR with no reachable human is load, whatever generated it.

The Unsolved Parts

Slop detection tooling is unreliable, disclosure is honor-system, and volunteer maintainers with forty open PRs drown no matter what the template says. None of this is solved. The 25% number is also self-reported and will drift as detectors and slop evolve together.

Maintainers: what share of your PRs this month would you call slop? And what's the one question that filters them fastest in your projects?

References

  1. Linux Foundation 2026 developer survey as reported (52% authoring speedup, 25% of PRs flagged as slop): tech-insider.org
  2. Jeff Geerling on the maintainer-vs-agent harassment case: jeffgeerling.com
  3. GitHub's PR caps for outside contributors: coderabbit.ai

articles.title: Why Nvidia Put Mamba and Attention Together for Agents
articles.description: Nvidia published the technical report for Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning this week. Super is a...
articles.body_html:
Nvidia published the technical report for Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning this week. Super is a 120-billion parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 12 billion active parameters per token, while Lightning is a 30-billion parameter model with 3 billion active parameters. On SWE-bench Pro, Super reached 51.78%, passing Nemotron 3 Ultra while activating roughly 4.6 times fewer parameters.

The architectural choice behind both models is an interleaved hybrid design combining Mamba-2 state space layers, sparse attention layers, and Mixture-of-Experts routing. Mixing state space layers with attention is an established approach, but in a multi-turn agent loop it targets an operational bottleneck that pure attention models struggle to handle.

The KV cache wall in agent loops

Anyone running autonomous coding agents knows the prompt profile looks nothing like standard chat. A single task often runs fifteen to thirty turns. Each turn passes system prompts, tool schemas, repository file trees, compiler outputs, and git diffs.

In a benchmark session, Nvidia evaluated a proxy workload of twenty turns, with 2,048 input tokens and 1,024 output tokens per turn. Under pure Transformer attention, the key-value cache accumulates every single token across the transcript. By turn twenty, each concurrent user consumes tens of thousands of cached tokens in GPU memory. When you serve multiple developer sessions simultaneously, memory bandwidth chokes and VRAM fills up before compute cores reach saturation.

Mamba layers handle long sequences differently. A state space model compresses history into a fixed-size recurrent state. It processes input tokens sequentially with linear complexity, keeping memory consumption constant regardless of sequence length.

The problem with pure Mamba models has always been exact retrieval. When an agent needs to inspect a stack trace, look up a function signature fifty lines above, or copy a specific variable name from an imported module, attention mechanisms outperform recurrent states. Interleaving Mamba layers with attention heads keeps exact retrieval intact while offloading large portions of sequential history to recurrent state.

The prefix caching catch

Managing state reuse inside the inference engine turns out to be more complex than model training.

In production agent serving, prefix caching is mandatory. You do not want to recompute system prompts and shared repository context on every turn. In pure attention models, engines like vLLM slice the KV cache into small per-token pages. If an incoming prompt matches an existing prefix, the engine attaches the matching cache blocks and begins generating immediately.

Hybrid models break this assumption. To resume execution at an arbitrary prompt position, the engine needs both the attention KV cache and the recurrent Mamba state at that exact boundary. That recurrent state contains the accumulated sequence summary for the entire layer, and it is significantly larger than an individual attention KV entry.

In vLLM, matching the byte size of Attention and Mamba cache groups means a single Mamba cache page occupies as many bytes as roughly 4,000 tokens of Attention KV cache. Retaining recurrent states at fine token intervals would consume too much memory, so the engine preserves Mamba checkpoints on coarse token boundaries.

When speculative decoding or agent branching rejects draft tokens, the execution pointer can roll back to a token position that does not align with a cached Mamba boundary. If the engine cannot find an aligned checkpoint, the scheduler has to split the prefill step, end at the nearest boundary, and execute an extra forward pass for the remaining tokens. That extra forward pass repeats kernel launches and tensor-parallel communication. Nvidia ended up patching vLLM in pull request 57329 to build internal prefill checkpoints so hybrid models could preserve prefix reuse without stalling the inference pipeline.

Why benchmark scores shift across harnesses

The paper also highlights how sensitive agent evaluations are to the harness running them. In Section 3.10, Nvidia tested Nemotron 3.5 Super across six agent harnesses on SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Running the exact same model weights produced noticeably different results depending on the scaffolding. Claude Code recorded 49.45% on SWE-bench Pro, while Codex recorded 61.80% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The rank order of harnesses flipped between the two benchmarks.

Developers often treat benchmark leaderboards as pure model comparisons. In practice, prompt scaffolding, tool output parsing, retry policies, and error handling change task success just as much as post-training. A model trained for tool calling will stumble if the harness wraps bash output in unexpected delimiters, and an average checkpoint can jump ten percentage points if the harness implements clean context pruning between commands.

What this means for local agent stacks

On GB200 systems, Nvidia reported serving throughput reaching 4,856 output tokens per second per GPU while keeping individual user latency above 50 tokens per second. That interactive threshold matters because developers will not wait two minutes for an agent turn to finish inspecting a directory.

Deploying agent infrastructure requires balancing compute and memory access. Pure attention architectures deliver strong reasoning, but their KV caches choke long agent sessions. Hybrid state space architectures offer a path to sustain interactive multi-turn sessions without drowning in cache memory, provided your inference engine knows how to manage recurrent checkpoints.

articles.title: Debugging at 3 AM: A Horror Story With No Villain Except Me
articles.description: Production was down, the dashboard was bleeding red, and every suspect had an alibi. The killer had...
articles.body_html:
Production was down, the dashboard was bleeding red, and every suspect had an alibi. The killer had my git credentials.
3:04 A.M.

The phone glows at 3:04 in the morning, and there is a grammar to that light. Not the white of a text from someone who loves you. Not the green of a package arriving. The amber of the paging app — the color of weather emergencies and furnace warnings; the color machines use when they want to inform you, courteously, that something you built is misbehaving in public.

I sat up in the dark and opened the laptop, which lit my face the way open freezers do in films about regret.

The dashboard was a Jackson Pollock painted entirely in red. Our authentication service — the front door of the product, the one service contractually obligated to be boring — was failing at a rate I had previously considered theoretical. Users weren't just failing to log in. They were being logged out. Mid-session, mid-sentence, all across the map, in every timezone our little empire covers.

Every engineer has a private horror story, and we tell them the way fishermen describe weather: exaggerated, semi-mythological, absolutely load-bearing. I want to tell you mine as what it actually was — a horror story — because it has every required element. A remote cabin (my apartment). A storm (rain, theatrical, unpaid). An isolated protagonist (me, insufferable). And a monster no search party could ever find, because I was about to spend four hours learning that the monster had my face and my commit history.

What it doesn't have is a villain. That's the part the genre never prepares you for.

The Fine Art of Needing Someone to Blame

Every incident has a casting call, and mine convened immediately.

Suspect one: the deploy. It is always the deploy; this is the closest thing software has to folk wisdom, and folk wisdom survives because it is usually right. I checked. Nothing had shipped in four days. The most recent release had the alibi of sediment.

Suspect two: the network. "It's not DNS," I told the empty room. "There is no way it's DNS." I checked the DNS anyway, the way you check behind the shower curtain in a horror film — not because you expect to find anything, but because the genre demands one token act of courage. The DNS was fine. Somehow its innocence felt like a betrayal.

Suspect three arrived on schedule, and I am not proud of this: the new engineer. She joined three weeks ago. She had shipped nothing, touched nothing, and was, at that moment, asleep like a person with a clear conscience — statistically the most suspicious condition there is. By 3:40 I had mentally drafted a post-mortem with her name in it. Gently worded. Professionally devastating.

Here is what I was actually doing, though I lacked the vocabulary for it at the time: running a comfort ritual. Humans are blame-seeking missiles. Hand us an unexplained catastrophe and we will generate a villain with the reflexive urgency of an immune response. Villains make chaos narratable. A system that failed for seventeen interacting reasons is a nightmare you can't repeat at parties; a system that failed because Dana pushed on Friday is a story, and stories feel like control.

The safety literature worked this out decades ago, in an industry that counts its dead. James Reason's Swiss cheese model — the one from aviation, the one that says disasters happen when the holes in several layers of defense happen to line up — exists precisely because "one careless person" is almost never the truth of a serious failure. Charles Perrow went further in Normal Accidents and argued that in systems complex enough, breakdowns are not anomalies at all. They're residents. They pay rent.

I knew all of this. I had once cited it at an all-hands, in a confident voice, with a slide. At 3:40 A.M., knowledge and comfort are different organs, and only one of them was working.

The Bug With a Bedtime

Salvation, when it came, came from the most suspicious direction available: arithmetic.

Coffee number three had arrived not as a beverage but as a coping mechanism with a handle. I stopped staring at the aggregate error graph — staring at aggregates at 4 A.M. is just doom with a scrollbar — and sliced the errors by hour instead.

And the error rate had a bedtime.

3:00 A.M. Sharp. A spike, a twenty-minute decay, silence. I scrolled back one day: 3:00 A.M., spike, decay, silence. Two days: the same. Seven nights, the same. A metronome wearing a ski mask. Whatever this was, it wasn't random and it wasn't ambient. It was scheduled. Something in my system looked at its watch every night, said now, and did a murder.

Naturally, it refused to happen in staging. I pointed every instrument I owned at the staging environment and it sat there, serene, error-free, smug in the way only a system without real traffic can be. For one feverish hour this felt like a genuine heisenbug — a bug that flees observation, a witness who heard a noise and declines to repeat it. Purists will object that an environment difference is not a true heisenbug, and the purists are right, but at 4:20 A.M. every bug that hides from daylight qualifies as uncanny.

I explained all of this, in detail, to the rubber duck on my desk. His name is Vladimir. He has heard things. He said nothing, which is his gift.

The clue that cracked it was almost embarrassing: the staging servers believed, sincerely and wholeheartedly, that they lived in UTC. The production servers lived in local time. Everything else was identical. Which meant the variable I had been treating as scenery — the clock — was the weapon.

Time zones are the Cthulhu of computing: ancient, tentacled, worshipped entirely by accident. Nobody believes in them until one reaches up out of the deep and takes a production system with it.

A Séance Called git blame

Follow the mechanics forward and the picture assembles itself with the awful neatness of a locked-room mystery finally solved.

The mass logouts came first. The errors were just the thundering herd of evicted users stampeding back toward the door. The logouts were evictions — something was deleting live sessions. And there was only one thing in the entire system with delete rights: a cleanup job, a cron, that pruned "expired" sessions every night while the city slept.

In its WHERE clause, the definition of expired was computed with one clock, while the sessions themselves had been stamped with another. For one window every night, the two clocks disagreed about whether it was still today — and during that window, the job scanned every live session in the database, judged them all ancient beyond recovery, and deleted them. All of them. Then it tidied up, logged its success, and went back to sleep until tomorrow.

And the schedule? The cron ran at 3:00 A.M., because 3:00 A.M. is when traffic is lowest. I know this with terrible intimacy, because I scheduled it there myself, a lifetime ago, in a pull request I described — I checked — as "safe."

One clock stamps. Another clock judges. Once a night, they disagree. The rest is arithmetic wearing a hockey mask.

I ran git blame on the comparison, which is less like forensics and more like a séance: you summon the dead, you ask who did this, and the answer always arrives in monospace. The blame lit up line by line, and then it landed on a commit from 241 days ago, with a message I have now read so many times I've stopped flinching:

quick fix: make cleanup behave for now, will revisit after launch

Author: me. Reviewer: me. And one line above it, written in my exact voice, a comment: // temporary, do not let this ship as-is.

I shipped it as-is.

I want to be precise about the feeling, because "the call is coming from inside the house" is a horror trope for a reason, and the reason is that the house is you. I read that code the way you reread a text you sent at a party: with dawning, pixel-by-pixel horror, at a stranger who had my name, my typing cadence, and my signature joke in the comments. I don't remember writing it. I remember launch week — I remember being exhausted and certain, which is the same memory wearing different clothes. Somewhere between then and now, that line stopped being mine and became the system's. Then the system handed it back to me at 3:04 A.M., with interest.

The Call Was Coming From Inside the Commit

Here is the thing I understood at around five in the morning, sitting in the wreckage of my own certainty — the thing I'd stay up all night again to keep:

A bug is not an intrusion. A bug is a disagreement — the residue left where the system in your head and the system in production quietly parted ways. Alfred Korzybski said the map is not the territory; code is a map we hand to a machine, and the machine is a perfectly literal client. It never rounds up toward our intentions. It executes the gap between what we meant and what we said — at nine digits a second, forever, until somebody notices.

And the noticing is science. Genuinely, structurally science. Every suspect I ran down that night was a hypothesis — the deploy, the network, the innocent new hire — and the logs were nature's answer: no, no, and no. Karl Popper would have recognized the procedure instantly. I wasn't debugging; I was falsifying. I was doing rigorous, disciplined science all night. I just hadn't expected the final theory to be me.

That's the twist the genre keeps missing. We tell debugging stories as detective stories — find the culprit, restore order, roll credits. But there is no culprit, because the culprit is a condition: complexity plus time plus a confident human moving quickly. Edsger Dijkstra — who never once let a good sentence go unsaid — put the quiet part loudly: "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence." Absence of bugs cannot be demonstrated. Only deferred. Every codebase is a haunted house where all the ghosts are future versions of the people currently alive.

Douglas Hofstadter wrote whole beautiful books about systems that contain their own self-reference — loops that point at themselves and turn strange. We ship those weekly. We just call it Tuesday.

So I gazed into the stack trace, and the stack trace gazed back into me, and it used my font.

Absolution Is Not a Deploy

The fix was one line. I want that on the record, because the disproportion is both the punchline and the lesson: a week of 3 A.M. pages, four hours of dread, one small theological crisis — resolved by teaching two clocks to agree. One word, effectively. Eight months of latent catastrophe, priced at less than a tweet.

Then I did the three things that actually mattered, none of which were the line of code.

I made staging's clocks match production's, because "works in staging" should at minimum mean "works on the same planet." I added an alert on mass logouts specifically, because error rates are the scream and logouts are the whisper, and monitors that only hear screams will always fail you at exactly the volume that matters. And I wrote the post-mortem, and I put my own name in the root cause field.

That last one is the bravest sentence in engineering: I did this. Not as penance. There were no robes, no ritual shaming, no wheel-of-misfortune slide at the all-hands. Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free — it means the consequence is knowledge. The document said, plainly: a well-meaning engineer, under launch pressure, shipped a temporary change with no ticket, no reminder, and no monitoring that could have caught it for 241 days. Remove any one of those conditions and the incident doesn't happen. Which means the fix was never "be more careful." The fix is "build a system where careful is not a heroic act."

Reason's Swiss cheese, again: I wasn't the hole. I was the unlucky alignment of the holes, wearing a lanyard.

At 6:40 the sun came up, indifferent, like a build that passes on the second try. I bought the new engineer a coffee and told her she'd been acquitted of a crime she never knew she was charged with. She laughed. Then she made me show her the diff, and she asked the question every senior engineer should be asked monthly:

"Who else has a TODO like this?"

We found four. Each had my fingerprints, or hers, or someone's — because that is what fingerprints are. Evidence that a human was here. And humans are how the future pages you.

Epilogue for the Next One

The next horror story has no villain either. Statistically speaking, it's you.

Not because you're careless — because you're fast, and confident, and navigating a map so much larger than any territory one person can hold. Seniority in this field isn't the accumulation of tricks. It's the slow, expensive process of updating your priors against your own evidence. Every scar is data. Every 3 A.M. is a peer review conducted by a merciless machine.

So, some benedictions — cheap, and hard-earned:

Write TODOs with dates, not vibes. Temporary, in production, means geological. Schedule your crons at hours you have personally witnessed while awake. And mistrust any diff you'd describe as "safe" in a pull request titled "small cleanup" — the monster is always introduced as a minor character.

The bugs of the future are being written right now, by people who are certain. The only defense our species has found is humility with instrumentation: assume the map is wrong, watch the territory, and when something finally pages you at 3 A.M., skip the séance. Open the blame. Say hello to the author.

Your turn: tell me about your 3 A.M. monster in the comments. I promise I won't ask who wrote it.

The answer is always the same.

articles.title: I Had No Idea What Was Eating My Mac’s Storage, So I Built Something to Show Me
articles.description: My Mac said 179.58 GB of 245.11 GB used. Applications made sense. Documents made sense. But a huge...
articles.body_html:
My Mac said 179.58 GB of 245.11 GB used. Applications made sense. Documents made sense. But a huge gray block labeled System Data took up more space than everything else combined, and macOS wouldn't tell me what was inside it.

I got tired of guessing, so I decided to build something that would show me everything and let me act on it. The next few days looked a lot like this:

How it came together

The first version was a plain CLI, built with a bit of help from my friend, AI.

It worked, but only just. It listed files under 10 MB, had no color, and nothing was organized.

So I went back and looked for libraries that could present the output properly, and rich was a big help. The second version was decent, but it still felt like something was missing.

Next I wondered whether the output could be interactive. It turned out I could connect a web interface to the Python side and route everything through it. That was a real improvement, but still not quite there.

A bit more digging showed me I could wrap that web interface in a native window. That's how it became a proper macOS app, which I built for myself first.

Then I opened Mac Deep Cleaner, the tool I'd made for exactly this problem, and let it scan my own machine.

It found a lot. More importantly, it showed me where every gigabyte lived, so I didn't have to guess. That's the whole idea: a cleaner that opens the box and lets you decide, instead of deleting things you never got to see.

The one rule

Never delete anything the user hasn't reviewed.

Everything else grew out of that sentence:

  • Files go to Finder's Trash, not straight into oblivion.
  • Before anything moves, every cleanup is checked against scan generation tokens, exact file IDs, inode matches, and path restrictions.
  • System files (com.apple.*, SIP-protected paths, running app bundles) are locked and can't be touched.
  • There's no cloud analytics. Everything runs on your machine.

What the scan found on my Mac

When you launch it, you get a local dashboard that tells you the truth right away.

Across 68 items, it found 34.63 GB that could be reclaimed. The split underneath that headline number matters more:

  • Safe to remove: 41.39 MB
  • Review first: 32.90 GB
  • Needs care: 1.69 GB

I could have made that headline far more exciting by auto-selecting everything. Instead, only the tiny safe slice is one click away. The big chunk is marked "Review first" because the tool can't know what matters to you, and I think that honesty is the whole point of the product.

Seeing inside your apps

The part I'm proudest of is the Application Analyzer. Pick any app and it shows the full footprint, not just the .app bundle.

Take VS Code, which uses 3.01 GB in total. The app bundle is 1.5 GB and Application Support is another 1.51 GB. The caches, the part that's truly regenerable, are only 2.28 MB. A lot of people assume clearing caches frees up gigabytes, and here you can see it doesn't. You get to decide with real numbers.

It also notices when an app is running and tells you to quit it before uninstalling. It's a small detail, but it saves you from a bad afternoon.

Under the hood

For the curious:

  • The core is Python 3.9+, installable with pip install mac-deep-cleaner.
  • A local web dashboard is served on a loopback port.
  • A Swift window shell provides native macOS chrome and full-screen support.
  • Scanning is multi-threaded, with content hashing for duplicate detection.
  • One tool, three commands: mac-deep-cleaner, mac-cleaner, and mdc.

What's new in v3.0.5

This release is all about polish, the things you only notice when they're wrong:

  • I fixed the missing top inset in browser mode, without disturbing native window and full-screen spacing.
  • The dashboard, favicon, README, and macOS icon now all use a single assets/app_icon.png, and I removed the redundant branding images.
  • Shared assets now ship in Python distributions and standalone macOS builds.
  • The CLI and native bundle versions come from one package version constant, so they can't drift apart.

Installing it

Option 1: Download the app (easiest)

Grab Mac-Deep-Cleaner-macOS.zip (about 9.7 MB) from the v3.0.5 release page.

Unzip it and drag Mac Deep Cleaner.app into your /Applications folder. Each release asset shows a SHA-256 checksum, so you can verify your download:

shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/Mac-Deep-Cleaner-macOS.zip

The output should match the checksum on the release page.

Option 2: Install with pip 

pip install mac-deep-cleaner
mdc

Option 3: Build from source 

git clone https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner.git
cd Mac-Cleaner
python3 scripts/build_mac.py

About the macOS warning

The downloadable app isn't notarized by Apple yet, so macOS may tell you it's "damaged" or can't be opened. It isn't damaged. Gatekeeper is just being cautious about a downloaded app that hasn't been notarized.

If you got it from the official release page, move it to /Applications and run:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Mac Deep Cleaner.app"

This only removes the download-quarantine flag from that one app. If you'd rather skip Terminal, right-click the app, choose Open, and confirm. Please only do this with builds from the official repo. Notarization is on my to-do list. (The pip install doesn't have this problem.)

What I learned

  1. Trust is a feature. Showing "Review first: 32.90 GB" instead of a giant green button made the tool feel more useful, not less.
  2. Boring consistency matters. One icon file, one version constant. Half of v3.0.5 was just deleting duplication.
  3. Local-first is a relief. No servers, no accounts, and nothing leaves your machine.

Try it, break it, tell me

It's open source under Apache 2.0:

  • Download: https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner/releases/tag/v3.0.5
  • GitHub: https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/mac-deep-cleaner/

If you find an app footprint it misses, or a path it should protect, open an issue. And if it frees up some space for you, a star helps more than you'd think.

So, what's the most surprising thing taking up space on your Mac?

Happing Coding ;)

articles.title: Is Rec Room Shutting Down? The Real Reason a $3.5B Platform Collapsed
articles.description: TL;DR    Rec Room is not "shutting down" anymore. It already did, at noon Pacific on June 1,...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • Rec Room is not "shutting down" anymore. It already did, at noon Pacific on June 1, 2026.
  • There was no single cause. The company said its costs "always ended up overwhelming the revenue we brought in."
  • It had 150 million+ players over a decade and a $3.5 billion valuation in 2021, but never became sustainably profitable.
  • Snap acquired "select assets" and some staff. The platform itself was not revived.
  • For developers, the lessons are about unit economics, moderation costs, and giving users an exit.

If you searched "is Rec Room shutting down?" this year, the answer changed from "maybe" to "yes" to "done" in about two months. The company announced the closure on March 30, 2026, and the servers went dark on June 1.

That is a strange ending for a platform that reached more than 150 million players and was valued at $3.5 billion in its December 2021 Series F. This article pulls together what the company and the press have actually said, separates confirmed facts from speculation, and draws out what developers building user-generated content (UGC) platforms can take from it. Everything here is current as of October 30, 2026.

What happened, in order

The collapse took about 15 months from the first layoff to the final shutdown.

Date What happened
Jun 1, 2026 Servers go offline at noon Pacific. The rec.net site closes, and an end-credits video is published.
May 18, 2026 Creators stop earning tokens; a final creator payout follows on June 1.
May 1, 2026 Token purchases end, and Partnered Creator registrations stop. Refund requests open (May 1 to June 15).
Mar 30, 2026 Rec Room announces the shutdown. Snap confirms it acquired "select assets" and that some staff will join its Specs Inc. hardware subsidiary.
Aug 25, 2025 About half of the staff are cut (141 positions), leaving just over 100 employees.
Mar 2025 First layoff round, affecting 16% of staff.
Dec 2021 Series F at a $3.5 billion valuation. The company raised $294 million across six rounds in total.

Sources: the company's shutdown post, GeekWire's shutdown report, GeekWire on the Snap deal and Road to VR on the 2025 layoffs.

The real reason: there wasn't just one

Headlines love a single villain, but the public record points to several problems stacking up. The company's own summary was blunt: it "never quite figured out how to make Rec Room a sustainably profitable business," and it blamed "the recent shift in the VR market, along with broader headwinds in gaming."

Here is what the reporting adds.

Popularity did not equal revenue.

The 150 million figure counts players over a decade, not people logging in today. The company said millions still played monthly, far fewer than the headline number. A free-to-play social hub still pays for servers, moderation and live operations for every active user.

The platform tried to be everything.

In its August 2025 layoff post, the company said its goal of a creation platform across VR, PC, consoles and mobile proved too ambitious. Mobile and console users produced millions of creations, but they were generally low-quality and poorly optimized, which strained the team. Co-founder Cameron Brown said the company was "narrowing our focus away from 'everyone can create' in favor of serving our very best creators," and described the company as too small for the universal vision but too big to pivot quickly.

Creator revenue grew, but not enough.

According to GeekWire, UGC revenue grew about 70% year over year as of September 2025, and creators earned more than $1 million in a single quarter for the first time. But Rec Room kept about 30 cents of each UGC dollar versus 70 cents on first-party content, so the fastest-growing line was also the thinnest.

AI features may have cost more than they earned.

GeekWire's report says per-user AI costs exceeded subscription revenue. That claim is the reporter's own narration with no date or named source, so treat it as a signal rather than a number.

What we still don't know.

Rec Room never published detailed financials. Nobody outside the company can say how close it came to a different outcome, so be wary of any post, including this one, that claims to know the one true cause.

What it meant for creators, players and staff

A shutdown tests a platform's promises. Here is how Rec Room handled the exit, based on its own announcement.

Creators lost new monetization immediately after the March announcement and stopped earning tokens on May 18. A final creator payout was processed on June 1. Working copies of rooms could not be downloaded once the servers went offline, so creators had to export room and invention data through the Steam PC build before June 1. After the announcement, a small internal team also built tools to export rooms and avatars in standard file formats, GeekWire reported. Road to VR noted that creators could use the exports to recreate rooms in Unity.

Players could no longer spend tokens after June 1. Gift cards were redeemable until April 30, refund requests for unused wallet funds ran from May 1 to June 15, and subscribers on three-, six-, and 12-month Rec Room Plus plans were refunded for unused time. Monthly subscribers had to cancel recurring payments themselves.

The community did not wait for an official successor. GeekWire reports that players uploaded their in-game report cards to fan sites to sign like yearbooks, and that unofficial fan-run servers are trying to keep versions of the game playable. No official successor was announced, and VRChat's co-founders said it "is not going anywhere."

Staff was split. Some joined Snap's Specs Inc. unit, while others are listed on a "Rec Room Grads" site seeking new roles. Snap has not disclosed how many people it hired, what it paid, or exactly which assets it bought.

Seven lessons for developers

These are my takeaways from the public record, not claims Rec Room made about itself.

  1. Track active users, not lifetime users: 150 million lifetime players and "millions" of monthly players are very different businesses. Put active users and cost per active user on your main dashboard.
  2. Count moderation as a core cost: UGC platforms pay for every creation someone uploads, whether anyone plays it or not. Rec Room said reviewing low-quality content strained its team.
  3. Know your take rate before you scale it: If the fastest-growing revenue line keeps 30 cents on the dollar and your biggest cost line grows with users, growth alone will not close the gap.
  4. Treat AI features as cost of goods sold: If inference cost per user can exceed what a subscription brings in, as GeekWire reports for Rec Room, price the feature or cap its usage before launch.
  5. Narrow the platform early: Supporting VR, PC, console, and mobile multiplied the surface area for bugs, content, and support. Each platform needs its own quality bar.
  6. Build the exit path before you need it: Rec Room built export tools after it announced the closure, with a hard deadline attached. If you run a platform, ship open-format export while you still have a full team.
  7. If you build on someone else's platform, keep your source outside it: Creators who held assets in standard formats could move on more easily. Everyone else depended on an export window that closed on June 1.

None of this means UGC platforms cannot work. It means the numbers have to work at the scale you are actually at, not the scale on your pitch deck.

The bottom line

Rec Room is gone, and the cause was ordinary rather than mysterious: a large audience, a cost base that grew with it, and revenue lines that never caught up. The company says it "spent a long time trying to find a way to make the numbers work." For the people who built rooms there, the loss is real even without a villain.

Your turn: have you built on a UGC platform that shut down or changed its rules? What would you have wanted exported, and when? Tell us in the comments.

Sources

  • School's Out for Rec Room (official announcement)
  • GeekWire: Rec Room shutting down, once valued at $3.5B
  • GeekWire: Snap acquires assets from Rec Room
  • GeekWire: Rec Room's final day
  • GeekWire: Rec Room lays off half its staff
  • Road to VR: layoffs and low-quality content (Aug 2025)
  • Road to VR: shutdown and Snap report
  • Fast Company: shutting down despite 150 million users
